items.descriptionOriginal: This article has been published in partnership with SBI Life Insurance. SBI Life Insurance believes in liberating individuals to pursue their aspirations while taking care of their loved ones. This belief is reflected in its core brand philosophy, 'Apne Liye, Apno Ke Liye'. At Glasgow 2026, the journeys of India's para-athletes brought this philosophy to life, showing how the support of family, coaches and those who stand beside us can make the difference between a dream and a medal. "When I had a polio attack, people forgot that my name was Avinash Kumar. They started calling me Jhandu Kumar, and many laughed at me." For years, Jhandu sold vegetables by the roadside. Whenever he found time, he would borrow a phone and teach himself bodybuilding through YouTube. There was no gym, no formal training and no coach — only a boy who refused to give up on the dream of becoming an athlete. But Jhandu's journey was never his alone. His family supported his ambition, local coaches recognised his potential, and eventually, a national coach gave his talent the direction it needed. But Jhandu's journey was never his alone. His family supported his ambition, local coaches recognised his potential, and eventually, a national coach gave his talent the direction it needed. Photograph: (SBI Life) At Glasgow 2026, that journey culminated in a Commonwealth bronze medal. For Sharmila Dhankar, sport became a way to reclaim a part of herself. "Since childhood, every person dreams of achieving something in life. Some achieve it through academics, while others find success in different fields. It took me 40 years to reach this point. And receiving this medal has given me a new direction in life." For decades, Sharmila put everyone else first — through a difficult marriage and while raising her two daughters on her own. Somewhere along the way, she picked up shot put and found something that was entirely her own. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) At 40, she made history by winning India's first-ever para-athletic gold at the Commonwealth Games. And for Dilip Mahadu Gavit, running began with something much simpler: a childhood love. After losing his right arm in a tree-fall accident at the age of five, Dilip grew up working on farms with one arm. But he never stopped running. When he eventually left his small village and came to the city to run, a coach noticed his speed and invited him to train. At Glasgow 2026, Dilip repaid that faith by winning a record-breaking gold. (Photograph: SBI Life) "I have loved running since childhood. When I came from my small village to the city to run, my coach saw me and asked me to come for training. He said, 'Come and train. We will see what you can do.'" That coach gave Dilip more than training. He brought him from his village and gave him a place to stay in his own home. "Whatever I am today is because of my guru. He brought me from my village and kept me in his own home." At Glasgow 2026, Dilip repaid that faith by winning a record-breaking gold. Three athletes. Three very different journeys. Yet their stories share something powerful: none of them reached the podium alone. Behind Jhandu was a family and coaches who saw an athlete beyond his circumstances. Behind Sharmila was the courage to make space for her own aspirations while carrying the responsibilities of her family. And behind Dilip was a coach who saw potential, opened his home and allowed a young runner to dream bigger. How SBI Life acknowledges dreams This is where SBI Life Insurance's 'Apne Liye, Apno Ke Liye' comes to life. The philosophy is built around a simple but powerful idea: our aspirations may be our own, but the journeys that take us towards them are often shaped by the people who stand beside us. SBI Life's partnership with the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) reflects this belief — supporting para-athletes as they pursue excellence, push beyond limitations, and chase bigger dreams. That commitment extends beyond the partnership itself. On 7 September, SBI Life brought together para-athletes at a felicitation event in Delhi, attended by SBI Life's leadership. The event reflected the brand's larger commitment to supporting para-athletes at the grassroots — not simply as a financial services provider, but as a partner invested in their journeys, aspirations and pursuit of excellence. At the event, Amit Jhingram, MD & CEO, SBI Life Insurance, shared, "When the athletes are pursuing their dreams, they put in a lot of hard work with a lot of determination, but it is not only their hard work. It is also the support that their families, their coaches, and their entire ecosystem provide to them. And this is what gels with the philosophy of SBI Life. This is truly "Apne Liye, Apno Ke Liye." Despite their vast & different journeys, one thing remains constant: an unwavering determination to pursue their dreams, often strengthened by the support of people and institutions who believe in their potential. (Photograph: SBI Life) For athletes like Jhandu, Sharmila, Dilip and four others – Shilpa Shyla, Mohammed Basil, Soman Rana, Shubham Juyal, a medal represents far more than a moment on the podium. It carries the faith of families, the guidance of coaches, and the support of people who chose to believe in their potential. And that is what makes their victories bigger than individual achievements. "For SBI Life, these athletes are 'Anokhe Heere'. It is a recognition of their achievement, of their success and their story. It's about their determination. It is about their sacrifice," said Ravindra Sharma, EVP and Chief of Brand, Corporate Communications and CSR, SBI Life Insurance. The partnership culminated in Japan But these stories of resilience extended far beyond Glasgow. In October, India's para-athletes competed at the Asian Para Games in Aichi–Nagoya, Japan, bringing a remarkable diversity of experiences from serving in the Indian Army and overcoming life-altering injuries to navigating financial hardships and rediscovering confidence through sport. Despite their vast & different journeys, one thing remained constant: an unwavering determination to pursue their dreams, often strengthened by the support of people and institutions who believe in their potential. This determination resulted in a record-breaking haul of 114 medals for the Indian contingent in Japan. It is this belief in the power of individual aspirations — and in the people who help make them possible — that lies at the heart of SBI Life Insurance's 'Apne Liye, Apno Ke Liye' philosophy. Through this partnership, SBI Life acknowledged the achievements of India's para-athletes, recognising not just the laurels they brought to the nation, but also the resilience, determination and collective support that made these accomplishments possible.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Generates Clean Energy, Saves Land, Improves Fishing—What’s Not to Like? Reading Time: 2 minutes In September 2026, solar developer D3 Energy installed a large solar array, not on land or on a rooftop, but on the surface of a reservoir that serves the water needs of the village of Monroeville, Ohio. This floating power plant covers 12 acres of the reservoir’s 16 acres. If a solar facility of this size, which contains 9,220 solar panels, were built on dry land, it would require 30 acres. So doing it the Monroeville way helps to keep open land available for farming, housing, business or industry, conservation land, or any other use. This 6-megawatt installation is projected to generate about 7,500 megawatt-hours of clean electricity to this village of 1,300 residents. Monroeville has already operated a 4-megawatt ground-mounted solar array, built in 2017. This 10-megawatt total gives the town roughly 13 times as much solar-generated power per capita as the rest of Ohio. Their floating solar array is among the five largest in the U.S. In addition to the clean power produced and the avoidance of using land that might be put toward other needed uses, Floato-voltaics projects such as this one have several other benefits. First, the physical barrier created by the floating platforms significantly reduces water evaporation by blocking direct solar radiation and intercepting wind blowing across the water’s surface. Solar “on the water” thereby reduces evaporation by 30% to 80%, depending on temperatures and humidity in the immediate area. The result, depending upon the size of the floating power plant, is an annual savings of millions of gallons of valuable drinking and irrigation water. Beyond clean power, floating solar arrays like Monroeville’s reduce reservoir water evaporation by 30% to 80% by blocking direct solar radiation and wind, saving millions of gallons of drinking and irrigation water annually. Photo courtesy of D3 Energy . Second, by depriving the water of sunlight, there is a sizable reduction of toxic algal blooms. Photosynthetic organisms like blue-green algae require sunlight to thrive. By heavily shading parts of the reservoir, the concentrations of floating solar panels limit the light penetration needed for massive algal blooms. This naturally improves water quality, reducing expenses from chemical treatments needed to purify the water. Third, more fish. During the warmer months, the floating platforms insulate the reservoir’s water against seasonal temperature spikes, helping support cold-water fish species. Local reservoirs are often favorite local fishing spots. And fourth, cleaning issues. Land-based solar arrays, whether in farming or more urbanized areas, often deal with dust, dirt, and other airborne debris. For best panel performance, cleaning of their surfaces in these situations is advisable. Open bodies of water are inherently less affected by blowing dirt and dust, keeping the panels cleaner longer and reducing maintenance costs. All things considered, with all the bodies of fresh water dotting the planet, maybe we should all look more closely for floato-voltaic opportunities just beyond our own backyard. The post Generates Clean Energy, Saves Land, Improves Fishing—What’s Not to Like? appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Προσπαθήστε να αλλάξετε τη μάχη του Hastings t…
items.descriptionOriginal: I n the early-ish days of Wikipedia, my college friends and I had an ongoing contest to see who could introduce a lie into an entry that would stick the longest. If your goal is to smuggle mistruth into the internet’s encyclopedia, you quickly learn to leave the well-known stuff with hard-and-fast facts alone. Try to change the Battle of Hastings to 1068, or claim Thomas Jefferson wrote Flowers for Algernon , and the Wiki editors swoop in to excise your lies within minutes. It was oddly inspiring to see that the online compulsion to be right, and for things to be right, could become a kind of immune system for upholding the truth. Observing the editors’ behaviors, I conjured up a new strategy. I found a less-trafficked page — the entry for club sandwich — and located a sentence that was already conjecture, and which notably had a citation affixed to its end. The line read: It is thought that the club sandwich was invented in an exclusive Saratoga Springs, New York gambling club in the late 19th Century. I changed this by adding my buddy Danny as the sandwich’s inventor: It is thought that the club sandwich was invented in an exclusive Saratoga Springs, New York gambling club in the late 19th Century by a maverick line cook named Danny Mears. It’s unlikely that John McPhee had stumbled across our Wikipedia sandwich lie when he wrote that “any error is everlasting” in his 2009 New Yorker piece about the magazine’s fact-checking department. But he was right. “Maverick line cook Danny Mears” hardened into sturdier fiction with each repetition, appearing in poorly researched blog posts and online recipes, each mention making the lie seem more true. Wiki editors pulled it down a few times; we snuck it back in. In the end, Mears’ reign as the sandwich’s inventor persisted on Wikipedia for more than three-and-a-half years. An annoyed editor even added a Wiki “talk” comment exposing our misdeeds, titled Danny Mears Did Not Invent It . A couple years later, a friend texted the group to say she’d seen “maverick line cook Danny Mears” go up on the flatscreens as a bar-trivia answer. McPhee goes on to describe the job of fact-checking as a kind of noble guardian, holding back a teeming horde of mistruths: “With drawn sword, the fact-checker stands near the end of this bridge.” We’d camouflaged our lie past a few of these sentries for what amounted to a joyride, but eventually the guards got us. What I’ve been wondering ever since, and especially lately, is: Who’s still guarding that bridge? O ne may initially concede that our defenses seem to be diminishing in the present moment. You don’t have to look far to find a commentator mourning a “post-fact” world or worrying that we swim in toxic waters online when it comes to bad actors and misinformation. Consider that 20 percent of Americans surveyed by Pew Research said they regularly get their news from TikTok, up from three percent in 2020. Last year, Meta ended its U.S. fact-checking program, while the courts have decided that social media platforms are private providers of forums for speech and so can set their own content rules, or remove the guardians from the bridge entirely, depending on their business incentives. Credit: patpitchaya / Shutterstock There are few forces more powerful in the media than a stubborn person on the phone investigating a doubt. In the public sphere of reportage, Duke Reporters’ Lab, which has tracked fact-checking trends for years, found that last year was the first time fact-checking department closures outpaced launches . And on the level of the individual, three-fourths of the fact-checkers surveyed by the International Fact-Checking Network reported being financially vulnerable or in crisis . If the field has had a famous debunker in the last two decades, it has been t he Washington Post ’s Glenn Kessler, who last year accepted a buyout and was not replaced. Should you want to pre-write a eulogy for the capital-T Truth, the material is all here. But fact-checking is not a static field. Like our immune systems, it’s capable of learning and enduring, as well as mobilizing to handle infections of mistruth, which if not treated tend to further polarize voters in political contests. Consider recent false claims from his opponents that Texas Senate candidate James Talarico had disappeared from the campaign trail for mental health treatment at an inpatient facility in Ohio. A high-profile fact-check quickly shifted the narrative from “Talarico is in trouble” to “his opponents look like liars.” (Talarico had the flu and was resting at home, which the New York Times proved by reviewing security camera footage.) Bad-faith punditry has a lessened effect when met with undeniable facts and data, as do the rumors that chip away at our trust in elections themselves. Consider a recent viral video in which a woman from Cook County, Illinois claimed that her voting machine was telling her that her chosen candidate was the less-popular choice. Nonpartisan fact-checks from places like PolitiFact quickly rushed to explain the less-salacious reality: She hadn’t selected enough candidates. Fact-checks can bring the temperature down and reduce our polarization; her town’s Republican Committeeman even rose to refute the claims on Facebook . So while the institutional layer of the media is wounded and we’re ushering in an age of slop and lies, any obituary for the Truth is likely premature. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] “Ever since I was a little kid, I’ve had a thing about wanting to get stuff right,” says Jy Murphy, a freelance fact-checker for the Hearst stable of publications and others. “At this point it bleeds over as a kind of professional deformity.” Murphy tells a simple story set years ago, in which he was fact-checking a Popular Mechanics piece about the freight industry and encountered a confident sentence claiming that nobody double-stacks rail cars in the Eastern U.S. because the bridges were all built with too little clearance. Fact-checkers encounter these offhand assertions all the time: a just-so statement with the ring of a thing that everybody knows. If you were to Google this type of niche knowledge, you might not find anything, and so the fact-checker operates most often as a reporter of the reporting. But after calling the railroad lines themselves, Murphy learned that in the year since the writer had filed the piece, a considerable number of bridges had been raised to allow freight through. The writer’s claim was “either too pessimistic to begin with or had changed in that year,” says Murphy. There are few forces more powerful in the media than a stubborn person on the phone investigating a doubt. It is precisely that thoroughness that makes peer-to-peer fact-checking matter more now in the age of A.I. Of course most large language models (LLMs) can’t yet make phone calls to freight lines, but if I ask Claude about Murphy’s rail bridges I may well still be told that nobody double-stacks rail cars in the Eastern U.S. That model can create a convincing, seemingly well-sourced sentence in a few seconds, but what it is not doing is actually checking the fact . Kelsey Lannin, a Seattle-based fact-checker, tells me that A.I is “very good at aping a confident intellectual on any given topic. But do any amount of work with it and you’ll quickly realize it’s a facade.” She says that it’s better to look at it like having an intern: “You give it an assignment, it gives you something back, and you [still] have to check it.” A.I. boosters may tell you that we’re just getting started, and assure us that this is the worst A.I. will ever be. Nevertheless, A.I. is still failing to produce accurate citations in more than 60 percent of tests, according to a 2025 Tow Center study . Prominent critics say it has nuked the effectiveness of Google and is “ destroying search, the internet and your brain. ” Models create a texture of verification, but they aren’t doing the analog process that makes verification real. If you see a bird out of your window, you can grab an Audubon guide and verify it. Feed a picture of that bird to an LLM and that model is neither “seeing” the chickadee nor “reading” from a primary source specifically. Models produce the most statistically likely next words, but unless prompted, there isn’t a step where Claude or Gemini confirms the truth of its response against the truth of the world. Credit: Andrey_Popov / Shutterstock Fact-checking’s collective response to changing times will continue to be a necessary governor, helping pace our accelerated information environment and dismantle false narratives that fuel polarization. These individual hallucinations and absent citations might seem like drops in a bucket, but they add up to create a rising tide of mistrust in a society already wary of the truthfulness of mainstream media . “What grieves me,” says Murphy, “is how many people think there aren’t [trusted sources].” Still, it is encouraging to see the fact-checking infrastructure responding by adapting to, and building defenses against, this flood. Sometimes, resistance looks like digging in. Inside the same Reporters’ Lab census that tallied closures, we learn that we’ve still got 437 active fact-checking projects around the world, which is just 27 below the all-time high and more than were operating in 2020. Many American newsrooms (North Dakota News Cooperative, CT Mirror in Connecticut and more) have agreed to work with Gigafact , an organization that publishes independently verified “fact briefs.” Wikipedia adopted a stronger A.I.-generated content policy earlier this year, banning LLM-generated content on the site, bar in certain circumstances. And as something becomes perceived to be scarce, it also becomes valuable: A 2026 Reuters study points toward an “increased demand for verification” from readers in a low-trust environment. The most encouraging turn of resistance may be in redirecting the machine back at the onslaught itself. Full Fact , the U.K.’s independent fact-checking charity, is now using A.I. systems to “detect and classify claims across millions of sentences,” per Reuters . A newer version attempts to “prebunk” instead of debunk, creating a model that prioritizes the most potentially damaging narratives for review. A Joint Research Centre study published in Nature investigated and concluded that debunking and prebunking interventions were successful and effective in reducing misinformation’s threats. Like any effort in inoculation, this effort will also need to be collective. At the end of last year, Scott Klein, then-publisher advocate at Newspack, predicted a “return to prioritizing open source collaboration, not as a luxury but as an existential imperative,” highlighting the need for a “show your work” ethos that will help journalism rebuild trust. Full Fact’s tools are being used now by more than 40 organizations across 30 countries, and importantly, the effort is mostly triage. Full Fact offers that the organization will “always keep human experts in the loop, partly to minimise the risks around bias and hallucinations that come with fully-automated systems but mostly because even the most advanced A.I. does not come close to human reasoning.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Sierra Juarez, a fact-checker at NPR’s Planet Money and The Indicator , has another, simpler tip for resistance in the world of misinformation. “If you see something on your social media feed that your gut is telling you seems fishy,” she says, “try to find corroborating evidence in three different sources across different types of publications. Read broadly and try to identify common threads.” Bringing the fact-checker’s stubborn doubt to our daily engagement is available to anyone willing to take a minute before they share a post. Years after my Wikipedia crime spree, I’m heartened that there are fact-checkers out there guarding the bridge and encouraged by the durability of this work. Reports of the Truth’s demise have perhaps been greatly exaggerated. It can be slow and unglamorous, but fact-checking’s collective response to changing times will continue to be a necessary governor, helping pace our accelerated information environment and dismantle false narratives that fuel polarization. “There are,” says Murphy, “good soldiers … a cadre of us out there trying to fight the good fight.” The post Truth, Elections and the Questionable History of the Club Sandwich appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Halloween may be known for its pumpkins, costumes, and haunted tales — but India has long celebrated its own versions of mystery and magic. Across the country, lamps glow through the night, dancers take on the forms of spirits, and stories of the unseen are shared by firelight. From Bengal's Bhoot Chaturdashi to Kerala's Theyyam , every region adds its own rhythm to this timeless fascination with light and darkness. Some mark the changing season, others honour folklore , but all capture that same mix of wonder and warmth — proof that India's festive calendar has its own kind of Halloween spirit. Though it may not be about trick or treating, wearing spooky costumes, or lighting pumpkins, these festivals draw striking parallels with Halloween — connecting people to folklore, community, and the idea that light always finds a way through darkness. Here's a look at five Indian traditions that echo the essence of Halloween, each with its own story, symbolism, and seasonal charm. 1. Bhoot Chaturdashi , also known as Bengali Halloween (West Bengal and Eastern India) When: A day before Diwali What people do: Families light 14 lamps at dusk to keep negative energies away. The lamps are placed in corners, near windows, and around the tulsi plant — illuminating every shadowed space in the home. It's also a night of storytelling, when elders share tales of ancestors and friendly spirits, filling homes with both curiosity and comfort. Why is it like Halloween? The festival centres around spirits and protection, much like Halloween's idea of keeping the dark at bay through light and play. 2. Kati Bihu (Assam) When: October / Around Diwali What people do: In rural Assam, Kati Bihu marks the transition between seasons and the start of the new agricultural cycle. Villagers light small lamps on bamboo poles in fields and granaries, hoping to protect crops from pests and bring good fortune to the harvest. Villagers light small lamps on bamboo poles in fields and granaries, hoping to protect crops from pests and bring good fortune to the harvest. (Image courtesy: assamtribune.com) This year, Kati Bihu coincided with Dhanteras , adding a shared glow across homes and fields. Why is it like Halloween? Though it celebrates the harvest, its essence lies in guarding against harm and illuminating darkness — an echo of Halloween's symbolic warmth amidst the chill. 3. Kartik Purnima (across North and West India) When: November What people do: As the full moon rises, rivers shimmer with hundreds of floating lamps. Families and communities gather near the water to celebrate light, gratitude, and the changing season. The night has a serene yet mystical feel — where reflection meets festivity, and the soft glow of lamps paints a picture of unity and peace. Why is it like Halloween? The moonlit night, glowing lamps, and celebration of transition carry the same sense of wonder that makes Halloween nights unforgettable. 4. Bhoota Kola (Tulu Nadu – Coastal Karnataka) When: Between December and May What people do: In the coastal districts of Karnataka, Bhoota Kola brings folklore to life through dramatic all-night performances. Performers, often from hereditary families, embody local spirit figures known as bhootas through elaborate costumes, striking makeup, and rhythmic dances. The event takes place under fire-lit skies and drumbeats, as villagers gather to watch tales of courage and justice unfold — part performance, part oral history. Why is it like Halloween? The transformation, the costumes, and the powerful night-time energy make Bhoota Kola India's own way of bridging the seen and unseen. 5. Theyyam (North Malabar, Kerala) When: October to May What people do: One of Kerala's most mesmerising ritual art forms, Theyyam combines dance, theatre, and transformation. Performers adorn vibrant face paint, ornate costumes, and towering headgear, embodying ancestral or mythic figures in a trance-like state. Like Halloween's symbolic costumes and storytelling, Theyyam celebrates transformation and mystery. The community gathers around as the performer, now in full transformation, narrates stories through movement, rhythm, and firelight — a living piece of folklore. Why is it like Halloween? Like Halloween's symbolic costumes and storytelling, Theyyam celebrates transformation and mystery — with its roots firmly planted in art and heritage. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Funding for Indigenous-Led Forest Conservation Gets a New Global Platform Reading Time: 3 minutes Funding for Indigenous-led forest conservation just became easier, as a new UNDP-hosted platform connects private companies and philanthropies directly with the communities protecting many of the world’s most critical forests. Funding for Indigenous-led forest conservation has long faced a structural gap. Indigenous Peoples steward roughly one third of the world’s tropical forests, yet they receive comparatively little political recognition or financial support for that role. Recent climate summits have repeatedly called for Indigenous access to forest tenure rights and climate finance, but turning those pledges into action has proven difficult. A new initiative, Forest Guardians Invest , aims to close that gap directly. Hosted by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the platform connects private companies, impact investors, and philanthropies with vetted Indigenous-led conservation and bioeconomy projects. Rather than routing funds through layers of intermediaries, the platform creates a more direct financial pathway. Tropical forests play an outsized role in global climate goals. These ecosystems support simultaneous action on climate change, biodiversity loss, and sustainable land management in ways few other landscapes can match. Protecting them effectively requires working with the people who already know these forests best. Many private companies and philanthropies are genuinely willing to fund forest protection through direct partnerships with Indigenous communities. What they typically lack is a reliable, efficient mechanism to do so at scale. Forest Guardians Invest positions itself as that missing mechanism, built specifically around respect for Indigenous rights and international standards. Three core functions define how the funding for Indigenous-led forest conservation platform operates. First, it facilitates financial partnerships between Indigenous Peoples and private companies, ensuring every agreement complies with human rights protections and recognized ESG standards. Second, it monitors private investments in Indigenous-led projects to confirm they deliver the environmental and economic outcomes both parties agreed upon. The platform’s third function focuses on long-term scale. Forest Guardians Invest builds a pipeline of bankable, Indigenous-led bioeconomy projects across forest territories, each with demonstrated climate, biodiversity, and economic results. That pipeline gives investors a clearer picture of opportunities beyond a single pilot project. Partnership models built around free, prior, and informed consent anchor the platform’s approach to Indigenous rights. This framework ensures Indigenous communities retain genuine decision-making power over how their territories and resources get used. Companies gain a trusted gateway to opportunities already vetted for impact and ethical compliance. One early example illustrates how this model works in practice. UNDP partnered with coffee company Lavazza to certify and market the first-ever deforestation-free coffee sourced from Ecuador. That pilot project is now being scaled to additional countries, offering a template for how similar partnerships might expand elsewhere. Harvesting coffee, part of a certified deforestation-free supply chain that shows what funding for Indigenous-led forest conservation can look like in practice. Photo by Carlos Felipe Ramírez Mesa on Unsplash. Founding partner Sacred Forests contributed both funding and a working model during the platform’s design phase. Their approach treats forest conservation itself as a service worth compensating directly, rather than folding it into broader carbon-offset accounting that often overlooks community-level impact. Seed funding from partners like Sacred Forests helped move Forest Guardians Invest from concept to functioning platform. The kind of on-the-ground work this funding for Indigenous-led forest conservation aims to support is already visible across the Amazon. In Brazil’s Maranhão state, a group of Guajajara women known as the Forest Warriors patrol more than 172,000 hectares of the Caru Indigenous Land. They monitor illegal logging, fight wildfires, and combine traditional ecological knowledge with modern tools like drones and GPS mapping. Efforts like theirs demonstrate both the value and the vulnerability of Indigenous-led conservation. Communities already carry out sophisticated, effective forest protection work, often with minimal external funding or formal recognition. Connecting that work to reliable financial support could meaningfully expand its reach and sustainability. Companies and philanthropies interested in engaging with the platform can apply to explore partnership opportunities directly through UNDP’s Climate and Forests initiative. Each partnership gets built around measurable outcomes, giving funders concrete evidence of the climate and biodiversity impact their investment produces. Funding for Indigenous-led forest conservation through platforms like this represents a shift in how global climate finance operates. Rather than treating Indigenous communities as beneficiaries of external programs, this model positions them as direct partners and innovators. That distinction may prove essential for protecting the forests the planet depends on most. The post Funding for Indigenous-Led Forest Conservation Gets a New Global Platform appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News New Map Reveals Natural Forest Regeneration in Tropical Regions Could Absorb 23 Years of Global Emissions Reading Time: 3 minutes A groundbreaking map identifies 215 million hectares suited for natural forest regeneration in tropical regions, capable of sequestering 23.4 gigatons of carbon. For decades, tree planting dominated forest restoration efforts worldwide, despite mounting evidence that a quieter, less expensive alternative often works better. Natural forest regeneration in tropical regions, allowing degraded land to recover on its own with minimal human intervention, frequently produces more biodiverse, resilient forests than plantation-style restoration under similar conditions. Until now, researchers lacked detailed, high-resolution data showing precisely where this natural recovery process holds the greatest promise. A Nature Ecology and Evolution study closed that gap, producing the first model mapping natural forest regeneration potential in tropical regions across every tropical forested country and biome on Earth. Built on remote sensing analysis identifying actual patches of natural forest regrowth between 2000 and 2016, rather than relying on coarse estimates or expert guesswork as previous studies had, the map offers unprecedented precision for targeting restoration investment. The results are striking. Researchers estimate 215 million hectares, an area larger than the entire country of Mexico, hold genuine potential for natural forest regeneration in tropical regions. Left to recover naturally over 30 years, this land could sequester an estimated 23.4 gigatons of above-ground carbon, roughly equivalent to more than two decades of current global emissions from fossil fuels and industry combined. Five countries account for more than half of this global potential. Brazil leads with over 20% of total regeneration potential, followed by Indonesia at nearly 14%, then China, Mexico, and Colombia, rounding out the top five nations that collectively represent 52% of the opportunity worldwide. This concentration suggests that even modest policy shifts within a handful of countries could unlock outsized climate and biodiversity benefits. What distinguishes natural forest regeneration in tropical regions from active planting is cost-effectiveness paired with ecological quality. Rather than purchasing seedlings, preparing sites, and maintaining plantations, natural regeneration often requires simply removing barriers preventing forest recovery, invasive species, unmanaged livestock grazing, or encroaching agriculture, then allowing existing seed banks, root systems, and nearby forest patches to do the rest. Research consistently shows this approach yields forests with greater species diversity and more resilient ecosystem function compared to plantation alternatives. Integrating Indigenous knowledge and securing land rights within these territories increasingly stands out as essential to translating mapped potential into genuine forest recovery. Communities that have sustainably managed these landscapes for generations bring practical understanding of local conditions that purely technical restoration planning cannot replicate on its own. Natural forest regeneration in tropical regions succeeds most reliably near existing forest patches and within territories managed by Indigenous Peoples, whose land stewardship researchers say is essential to translating mapped regeneration potential into genuine, lasting forest recovery. Photo by Bill Salazar on Pexels. The map reveals fine-scale spatial variation researchers say is critical for effective planning. Regeneration potential clusters strongly near existing forest patches, since seed dispersal and ecological connectivity heavily influence whether cleared land can recover naturally. This granular detail lets governments and conservation organizations distinguish between land where natural forest regeneration in tropical regions will likely succeed unaided and land that requires more intensive intervention or active planting. Beyond carbon sequestration, restoring tropical forests at this scale carries far-reaching consequences for biodiversity conservation, since tropical forests harbor a disproportionate share of Earth’s terrestrial species diversity. Millions of livelihoods across forested tropical nations also depend directly on healthy forest ecosystems for food, water regulation, and economic activity, so successful regeneration delivers benefits that extend well beyond atmospheric carbon accounting. Researchers emphasize that the map is intended as a decision-support tool rather than a final policy prescription. Natural forest regeneration in tropical regions succeeds only when paired with appropriate governance structures, including payment-for-ecosystem-services schemes and stronger frameworks that compensate communities for environmental stewardship. The overlap between high-potential regeneration zones and Indigenous Peoples’ territories adds further complexity, since these communities often lack formal land recognition despite serving as effective forest stewards in practice. As nations pursue ambitious global restoration commitments under frameworks addressing both climate change and biodiversity loss, this map offers something previously unavailable: precise, evidence-based guidance on where natural forest regeneration in tropical regions could deliver the greatest return on conservation investment. Rather than treating forest restoration as a uniform global strategy, the research points to a more targeted approach, one that recognizes that some degraded tropical land wants only the chance to heal itself, provided the barriers standing in its way are finally removed. The post New Map Reveals Natural Forest Regeneration in Tropical Regions Could Absorb 23 Years of Global Emissions appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Αυτό που ακολούθησε ήταν τρία χρόνια δύο…
items.descriptionOriginal: For 42 years, Peter navigated a world built on words he couldn't read -- memorizing road signs, mapping routes in his mind, quietly relying on his wife -- until a moment of panic in a supermarket aisle, afraid he might accidentally poison his family with the wrong milk, made it impossible to keep going as before. What followed was three years of twice-weekly sessions with a volunteer named Alison, working through reading manuals slowly and without judgment, until the world, as Peter puts it, "completely opened up." His goal had been to read the first Harry Potter book, drawn to Harry as a fellow outsider, and he finished it. The story sits with you not because of how far Peter came, but because of how long he carried something so heavy so quietly -- and how, in the end, it was a wife's steady presence, a stranger's patience, and his own willingness to try one more time that made the difference. "I can't believe how beautiful reading is," he says now, and the wonder in that sentence belongs to anyone who has ever arrived somewhere they once thought was not meant for them.

items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "India Invented This?" — The Better India's weekly trivia series that uncovers the Indian minds, ideas and innovations behind inventions that have shaped the way we live. From ingenious solutions created by scientists and engineers to technologies developed in response to some of India's biggest challenges, each story goes beyond the invention to explore the problem it solved, the impact it created and why it still matters today. On a winter morning in Delhi, the skyline can almost disappear behind a grey haze. The air feels heavy, eyes begin to sting, and even a short walk outdoors can become uncomfortable. For millions of residents, this is a familiar part of life during the city's pollution season. But what if scientists could predict when the air is likely to get worse — before the haze settles in? That is the question Dr Sachin Ghude, a scientist at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune, has been working to answer. Winter pollution can blanket Delhi in haze, making it harder for residents to breathe comfortably and increasing the need for timely air-quality warnings. Photograph: ( BBC) Ghude has played a leading role in developing India's Air Quality Early Warning System (AQEWS), which can forecast extreme pollution events in Delhi up to 72 hours in advance. Developed through a collaborative effort involving IITM, the India Meteorological Department and the National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting, the system gives authorities valuable time to prepare for deteriorating air quality. Predicting pollution before it arrives Air pollution is not caused by a single source. Vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, construction dust and crop-residue burning can all contribute to the problem. Weather conditions also play a crucial role: when winds are weak and the atmosphere prevents pollutants from dispersing, pollution can build up near the ground. Understanding how these factors interact is central to Ghude's work in atmospheric chemistry and air-quality modelling. Think of AQEWS as a weather forecast for the air we breathe. While a conventional weather forecast predicts rain or temperature changes, this system also calculates how pollutants are likely to move, react and accumulate in the atmosphere. AQEWS combines weather forecasts, satellite data, ground-based monitoring and emissions estimates to predict how pollution levels may change. Photograph: ( AQI.in ) To do this, it combines observations from ground-based monitoring stations with satellite information, weather forecasts and estimates of emissions from different sources. Advanced computer models then simulate how atmospheric conditions and pollutants may change over the next three days. The result is a forecast of air quality, including pollutants such as fine particulate matter (PM2.5), which can penetrate deep into the lungs. Why a 72-hour warning matters The system's biggest contribution is the time it gives authorities to respond. When pollution levels rise sharply, officials may need to consider measures such as restricting construction activities or curbing certain industrial operations under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP). A forecast issued in advance can help them prepare for these interventions instead of reacting only after air quality has deteriorated. The system was launched in October 2018 to predict extreme pollution episodes and provide early alerts. By forecasting severe pollution up to three days ahead, the system gives authorities time to consider preventive measures before air quality worsens. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) The science has also moved towards more detailed forecasts. IITM has implemented an operational air-quality forecasting model for Delhi at a resolution of 400 metres, using satellite and surface observations alongside advanced modelling techniques. This allows forecasts to capture local variations in pollution more closely than a single city-wide average. Such forecasts do not eliminate pollution on their own. Their effectiveness depends on how authorities use the information and how successfully they tackle the sources of emissions. Where is all this pollution coming from? Forecasting when pollution will worsen is only part of the challenge. Scientists must also understand where it comes from. Different pollution sources leave different chemical signatures. By studying these alongside atmospheric conditions, researchers can better estimate which sources contribute to poor air quality and help policymakers identify more targeted interventions. This is an important part of the broader scientific effort to make air-quality management more precise, moving beyond simply measuring pollution towards understanding what drives it. Studying the chemical signatures of pollutants helps researchers identify their likely sources and supports more targeted air-quality management. Photograph: ( IITM ) For Ghude, whose research connects atmospheric chemistry with air quality, human health, vegetation and climate, this work brings complex science closer to everyday public needs. A forecast cannot promise that tomorrow's sky will be clear. But knowing that pollution may worsen three days from now gives authorities an opportunity to prepare — and gives the rest of us a clearer picture of the air we are about to breathe. Sources: 'Dr. Sachin D Ghude' by ileaps 'Impact of Biomass Burning on Fine Aerosol Chemistry and Aging Processes in the Indo‐Gangetic Plain' by Sachin D Ghude for Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres. 'Delhi: Scientists look to trace exact source of pollution to help improve air quality' by Kushagra Dixit for The Times of India, Published on 29 January 2022. 'IITM releases documentary on air quality warning system for Delhi' by Indian Express, Published on 19 February 2021.

items.description: Ένας άντρας στο Μίσιγκαν περνούσε μια ιδιαίτερα δύσκολη μέρα. Ως υπάλληλος αργά το βράδυ στο κατάστημα παράδοσης για την πίτσα Red Baron, ο «Walt Z» δούλευε πολλές, εξαντλητικές ώρες, μάζευε πίτσα στον διάδρομο παγωμένου φαγητού. Ωστόσο, αυτό δεν τον εμπόδισε να χαιρετήσει έναν πελάτη με ευγένεια όταν του ζητήθηκε η ώρα. Τα πράγματα γρήγορα πήραν τροπή από εκεί. Σε ένα κλιπ που κάνει τους γύρους…
items.descriptionOriginal: A man in Michigan was having an especially hard day. As a late night store delivery worker for Red Baron pizza , “Walt Z” was working long, exhausting hours, stocking pizza in the frozen food aisle. Yet this didn’t stop him from greeting a customer with kindness when asked the time. Things quickly took a turn from there. In a clip making the rounds, we see him as he’s approached by a guy asking a question. When he pulls out his phone, the man “pretends” to steal ten dollars by using Apple Pay. Turns out the whole exchange had been a poorly thought-out “prank” from someone trying to get online clicks, and is filming/streaming the exchange live. View this post on Instagram At his wit’s end The worker was simply at his wit’s end. He essentially—and quite understandably—gets emotional and angry, as he pleads his case to the man filming. “Are you recording me right now,” he asks, while walking toward the front of the store. The streamer doesn’t let up, even when the employee seems visibly devastated. The streamer maintains that it’s “just a joke”. But it wasn’t a joke to this hardworking man. “It’s not a joke to me, okay? I don’t have time for this crap right now, okay? My life is hard enough as it is. I’ve got kids at home who went to bed without me right now.” He raises his voice, as his own words begin to hit home. “I was supposed to be home an hour ago. I’m still out here working. And I got to get up at 5 in the morning and do ten more stores! So this is not a joke to me!” Once it sets in that again, this is being filmed, he realizes there may be consequences. “And now I’m gonna get kicked out of the store BECAUSE OF YOU! Not funny!” The streamer apologizes, but it’s too late. The employee continues, “I’ve got a mortgage. And I’ve got four kids at home! So not funny!” It’s gut-wrenching to watch, maybe because so many of us have been there. Hanging on by a thread, trying to juggle our lives. Most likely, the prankster didn’t mean to set off such heavy emotions. But it’s a huge reminder that we never know what’s going on with someone on any given day. A wonderful turn But this story takes an incredible turn for the wonderful. Once the video went live, there was an outpouring of support for the employee. A man named Luke Oakenshield, without even knowing the worker’s name, started a GoFundMe in his honor. Oakenshield explains, “I do not know the worker personally and am actively searching for his contact information so I can make sure he receives the funds directly. Any aid in finding this man would be of the greatest help. I will not be receiving any of the money, as this is intended for the worker. God bless.” Standing up for the working person He also explains why he was so moved to help. “This fundraiser is about standing up for a working person who is busting their butt and should not have to fear losing stability because someone wanted content and clicks. If you can, please donate and share to help push back against rage-bait harassment and show this worker that people care.” Care, they did. In just a day, the GoFundMe at raised over $410,000 and it’s growing quickly. The page was updated to share they found the employee and that he’s over the moon. Oakenshield shares, “THE WORKER HAS BEEN FOUND! Walt Z out of Michigan sends a heartfelt thank you, and is absolutely blown away by how much people have cared over this. They are requesting privacy, and GoFundMe is taking the lead in transferring all of this to him. You’re all rock stars, and it shows.” Employee of the month But there’s more. Since there was fear that Walt might lose his job, Red Baron Pizza not only confirmed that he still worked for them, but that he was receiving the “employee of the month” title. They add, “He’s still here. He’s got a fan club. Including us.” View this post on Instagram It was just one of those days. Some online are calling it his Falling Down moment (referring to the film wherein Michael Douglas’s final straw is McDonald’s not serving breakfast after 10:00am). It didn’t end well for Douglas. But for Walt…now there’s proof that there are still total strangers who have his back. As for the content creator, reportedly he has deleted his social media. Perhaps this chain of events can have a positive effect on his life too. Who knows? Maybe Red Baron, who seem like a pretty standup company, is hiring. The post A Red Baron worker was devastated by a mean viral ‘prank.’ Strangers stepped in and changed his life. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: "Education can become a burden when a family has limited resources." For Paturi Namratha Siri, a student from Yernagudem village in Andhra Pradesh, there were times when continuing her education felt difficult . She did not always have the learning resources or support she needed after school. "Understanding some subjects was hard, and I needed additional guidance," she explains. Her experience is familiar to Bethala Veera Swami, who is now 58 years old and grew up in the same village several decades earlier. The village he remembers Born in 1968, he spent his childhood in Yernagudem, studying from Class 1 to Class 10. His parents were daily-wage agricultural labourers. The family had a small piece of land, but it was not enough to provide for everyone through the year. "My father and mother were daily-wage workers when I was growing up. They would go to the agricultural fields every day, and our family depended entirely on what they earned that day. This was the reality of my childhood," he tells The Better India . Some children entered the workforce. Others left school because there was little support at home. His parents nevertheless encouraged him to study. After school, he went to DNR College in Bhimavaram for intermediate and then joined the College of Engineering at Osmania University in Hyderabad, where he studied mechanical engineering from 1986 to 1990. He began his professional career in 1991 and spent the following decades working across India and overseas, including in Nigeria, Kuwait, and the UAE. Today, he works as a lead contracts engineer in Abu Dhabi. But while his career took him away from Yernagudem, what he had seen there stayed with him. "I saw children my age being pulled out of school, not because they lacked ability or ambition, but because their families could not afford to keep them there." Some children entered the workforce. Others left school because there was little support at home or because they had fewer opportunities to learn beyond the classroom. "What struck me most was the inequality of opportunity. The gap was not about intelligence or potential, but about access," he says. It started with a question among childhood friends In 2010, while spending time with childhood friends in Yernagudem, Swami began discussing how they could give something back to the community they had grown up in. Their answer was education. They wanted to 'gift education' to children they would later call V-Kids, beginning in their own village. On 13 January 2011, the Pragathi Association for Rural Development was registered as a society. The organisation later came to be known as PARD INDIA. Swami was already working abroad, and he continued his career while he and his friends began building the initiative around their existing jobs, local volunteers, and people from the communities they wanted to work with. The first programme was launched in August 2011 at the Government MPP Special School in Yernagudem, where Swami had studied. It began with 50 children from Classes 4 and 5. What happens when the school day ends? For many children in these villages, the challenge was finding someone to help them with their studies after school. Their parents often worked as agricultural labourers or in other daily-wage jobs, returning home late with little time to help with lessons. Swami and his friends wanted to address this gap. Their first initiative, the After School Education Programme (ASEP), gave children a place to continue learning with guidance once their regular school day ended. "Most of the children we cover have parents who work on daily wages. In the villages, they go to the fields and may not return until four, five, or even six in the evening," the founder says. ASEP runs from 3.30 pm to 5.30 pm, six days a week, offering children two hours of guided learning. They receive help with mathematics, English, science, moral education, and computer skills. They also make time for reading, sports, drawing, debates, competitions, storytelling, guest lectures, and tree plantation activities. Teachers monitor attendance and speak to parents when children begin missing classes. The programme is also meant to catch warning signs before a child drops out of school altogether. PARD INDIA tracks attendance and works with teachers, parents, and local volunteers when children are regularly absent. Swami says the organisation has found that the reasons are mostly tied to circumstances outside the classroom. "Poverty remains the biggest barrier to education. For families living on daily wages, education can feel like a luxury, and when they have to choose between sending a child to school and meeting immediate financial needs, education is frequently sacrificed," he explains. But money is not the only issue. "The challenge goes beyond finances," he adds. "Rural children are just as intelligent and ambitious as their urban counterparts, but they lack exposure, mentorship, digital access, and supportive learning environments." Bringing computers and new opportunities to villages The initiative gradually added other forms of support to address the different challenges that could interrupt a child's education. The Village Knowledge Centre Programme (VKCP) began in August 2012. At the time, internet access was still limited in many villages. Swami personally contributed Rs 8 lakh and helped establish a centre with 15 computers. Children could learn basic computer skills and use programmes such as Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. The centre operated for nearly eight years. Over time, the computers became outdated. The team now hopes to upgrade and expand the programme with CSR support and has approached several organisations for funding. Alongside computer lessons, the programme also offers career guidance and personality development sessions. For Swami, the idea was simple: children growing up in villages should have the same chance to learn new skills and explore career opportunities as children elsewhere. He wanted them to feel confident about their abilities and know that their circumstances did not have to limit their ambitions. Two years later, in July 2014, PARD INDIA launched the V-Kid Scholarship Programme (VKSP). In 2010, while spending time with childhood friends in Yernagudem, Swami began discussing how they could give something back to the community they had grown up in. The programme supports children who may otherwise struggle to continue their education because of financial circumstances, with particular attention to orphans, children of single parents, and economically disadvantaged families. Students apply according to set criteria, after which the organisation tries to connect eligible children with local donors. Support can extend from Class 1 through graduation. The team also runs the V-Kid Knowledge Boost Programme (VKKB), through which children are selected based on merit-based tests and receive longer-term scholarships. An Rs 800 scholarship and the confidence to continue In 2017, Vamisetti Ganesh from Devarapalli Mandal took part in one such examination. His parents were daily-wage workers, and paying for everything the family needed was not always easy. He secured fifth place in the VKKB examination and received an annual scholarship of Rs 800 for six years, covering his education from Class 6 to Class 10. The scholarship was supported by Mr Nageswara Rao, one of the donors. "Because my parents depend on daily wage work, meeting all our family and educational expenses has not always been possible," he says. The scholarship eased some of that pressure. "It helped with school-related expenses and reduced the financial burden on my family," he says. "It also motivated me to take my education more seriously and aim for better academic results." He is now pursuing his graduation. For Madhuri from Yadavolu village in East Godavari district, the scholarship provided similar continuity. She came from a family dependent on daily wages and received a six-year scholarship through the VKKB programme, covering Class 6 to Class 10. Today, she is pursuing intermediate education in Zangareddigudam and hopes to become an engineer. The difference is not always visible in a single examination result. Sometimes it means that a child keeps going to school the following year. 'I want to support people in need' For Yangala Uma Maheshwari from Gopalapuram, education became particularly difficult after she lost both her parents. She had been associated with PARD INDIA since she was six years old and had received support through the VKKB scholarship programme. When she lost her parents, the organisation continued to stand by her. "The most difficult period of my life began when I lost both my parents. Their absence left a void in my life, and I was suddenly faced with uncertainty, emotional pain, and the question of how I would continue my education without them," she explains. The support she received went beyond the scholarship. "During that difficult time, the team stood by me and provided emotional as well as academic support," she says. "Their continued care gave me the strength to keep moving forward." She is continuing her education and now wants to help other people facing difficult circumstances. "I want to support underprivileged and needy people, just as this organisation supported me when I needed help the most," she says. "I hope to become a source of encouragement and hope for others." From 50 children to over 110 villages What began with 50 children in Yernagudem has since spread across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. The non-profit now works in more than 110 villages and has influenced more than 550 communities. Its work has reached places including Cheepurugudem, Dubacherla, Nallajarla, Chinnayagudem, Devarapalle, Tyajampudi, Yadavole, Duddukuru, Goplapuram, Rajahmundry, Kakinada, Vijayawada, Abdullapurmet, Kuntloor in Hyderabad, Jafarguda, Rajivgruha Kalpa, Mathuguda, and rural clusters around Visakhapatnam. As of March 2026, the organisation reports 116,841 direct beneficiaries, including children and elders, and 90,494 V-Kids supported through its programmes. Its work has touched 492,567 lives through education, healthcare, nutrition and community empowerment. Within its education work, ASEP alone has provided 569,419 hours of free education to 3,165 children across 79 villages as of 31 March 2026. The Village Knowledge Centre Programme has delivered 33,999 hours of IT training to 538 children and young people. More than 30 students have received annual scholarships through VKSP. These figures cover different programmes, each addressing a challenge that can affect a child's education. A child should not have to leave school simply because there is nobody at home who can help with a difficult lesson, because the family cannot manage an educational expense, or because the child has never been shown what might be possible beyond the village. Namratha is one of the children still at the beginning of that journey. 'I want to become a district collector' Namratha, a Class 5 student, says her after-school classes helped her understand difficult lessons and gave her individual attention when she was struggling. They wanted to 'gift education' to children they would later call V-Kids, beginning in their own village. "Whenever I doubted myself, the teachers encouraged me and reminded me that I could do better," she says. Her confidence has changed too. "I have become more confident in my studies and in myself . Earlier, I would sometimes hesitate when I faced difficult subjects or challenges, but now I feel more comfortable taking them on," she adds. Today, she wants to become a district collector. "I want to complete my studies and build a successful career," she continues. "I also want to inspire other children to continue their education and never give up on their dreams." For Swami, these ambitions are precisely why the work needs to continue. "The greatest reward of this 15-year journey has been seeing children who were once at risk of dropping out now dream of becoming engineers, doctors, teachers, entrepreneurs, civil servants, and community leaders," he says. Keeping children in school takes a village Supporting these children across villages requires a network of people who can stay connected with them and their families. The initiative's work is supported by a 16-member executive committee, directors and advisers, brand ambassadors, project management teams, an IT team, and volunteer committees at the state, district, mandal (an administrative subdivision), and village levels. The founder puts the wider team at around 52 people, including full-time and part-time members, teachers, volunteers, and others involved in its programmes. There are currently around 20 project management team members and a four-member IT team, while the number of people working on individual projects changes according to their requirements. But a large part of the work rests with people who live in the communities themselves. Village committees help connect children, parents, teachers, and local volunteers. They also help identify children whose attendance is falling and encourage families to keep them in school. "This is the strength of our organisation," the founder says of its volunteer network. "Wherever we run the After School Education Programme, we make sure there is a village committee in place. We do not implement the programme without the committee's involvement." The organisation's model has allowed it to remain connected to villages even while Swami continues to work abroad. He brings his professional experience in planning, contracts, and project management into PARD INDIA, while the organisation keeps him connected to the place where he started. "My corporate career and social service journey complement each other," he says. "While my professional role challenges me to manage complex projects and think strategically, my work with this organisation keeps me grounded in the values of compassion, community service, and human impact." More villages, more scholarships and bigger dreams The initiative now wants to reach 20,000 children across 150 villages by 2030 and provide more than eight million hours of free education. It also plans to introduce STEM-based projects in government schools, expand scholarships from Class 1 through graduation, and develop Village Knowledge Centres with computer- and AI-enabled literacy and skills training. For Swami, the work has always been about more than numbers. ASEP runs from 3.30 pm to 5.30 pm, six days a week, offering children two hours of guided learning. "Education is the most powerful catalyst for social change," he says. He has spent much of his adult life working on large projects overseas, but the reason he continues to return to this work is rooted in what he saw as a child. "I firmly believe that lasting change must begin where we come from. Staying involved with the initiative is not just about leading an organisation. It is about honouring my roots, empowering V-Kids, uplifting families, strengthening communities, and making sure that no child's future is determined by poverty or circumstance," he explains. In Yernagudem, that idea now sits alongside a very different kind of future. Namratha is still in school. Ganesh is pursuing graduation. Madhuri is studying towards her next stage of education. Uma wants to help other children who face the kind of loss she did. Their journeys are different, but each began with the chance to keep studying. And that is what Swami has been trying to protect since that first conversation with his friends in January 2010. He wants every child to have the chance to stay in school long enough to decide what comes next. All pictures courtesy PARD INDIA.

items.descriptionOriginal: "How much did everyone else score?" For many teenagers, this question matters almost as much as their own marks. A friend has scored 95, a classmate is already preparing for the next entrance exam, and someone else seems to have everything figured out. Suddenly, their own result doesn't feel good enough. Even before the next exam begins, the pressure to keep up has already set in. What starts as a comparison of marks can soon become something more personal: Am I smart enough? Am I falling behind? Why does everyone seem to be doing better than me? For parents, these moments can be difficult to navigate. Telling a teenager not to compare themselves with others may seem like the obvious response, but what happens when they cannot stop? And how can parents help them build confidence without adding to the pressure? Why comparison feels so intense during the teenage years Dr Gurbani Kohli, a child and adolescent psychologist with over 11 years of clinical experience, has worked with more than 9,000 children. She is the founder and clinical director of HealG A Child Clinic and a senior consultant child psychologist at Apollo Cradle, New Delhi. Her work involves supporting children, adolescents, and families navigating developmental, emotional, behavioural, and learning concerns. In her experience, when teenagers compare themselves with their peers, the issue often extends beyond marks or achievements. Child and adolescent psychologist Dr Gurbani Kohli encourages parents to understand the emotions behind a teenager's comparisons rather than dismissing them. Photograph: (Gurbani Kohli) "When a teenager says, 'Everyone is ahead of me,' they are usually not making an objective assessment of everyone around them. They are expressing how they currently feel about themselves," she says. Adolescence is a period when identity and self-worth are still developing. Peers become increasingly important as teenagers try to understand where they fit in and how others perceive them. A disappointing exam result, a friend's achievement, or being left out of a group can feel particularly significant at this stage, when emotional regulation and perspective are still developing. "Often there is a deeper emotional question underneath the comparison: 'Am I good enough?' 'Do I belong?' or 'Will people value me and my opinion?'" Dr Kohli explains. A teenager who performs poorly in one exam may conclude that they are not good at academics altogether. Someone who misses out on an opportunity may interpret it as proof that they are falling behind. Understanding what lies beneath these conclusions is the first step towards helping teenagers navigate them. When marks become a measure of worth Academic competition can intensify these feelings because exam results are visible, easy to compare, and frequently discussed among families and peers. Questions such as "How much did everyone else get?" can shift a teenager's attention from learning to ranking. Even comments intended to motivate can add to the pressure. "Your sister got such good marks," "Look how well behaved she is" or "You used to do so much better" may leave a child feeling that they are being measured against someone else. When a friend performs better in an exam, a teenager may begin questioning their own abilities and self-worth. Photograph: ( iStock ) Dr Kohli advises parents to notice when comparison begins affecting a teenager's behaviour or confidence. Repeatedly saying they are "not good enough", giving up because they expect to fail, withdrawing from friends or losing interest in activities they once enjoyed are signs worth paying attention to. Some comparison is normal during adolescence. But when it starts shaping how a teenager sees themselves or interferes with everyday life, parents should look beyond the immediate trigger. Listen before offering reassurance When a teenager comes home upset because a friend scored better or secured an opportunity they wanted, a parent's instinct may be to offer perspective. They might say, "Don't be jealous", "You should be happy for your friend," or "There are so many children doing worse than you." Although well-intentioned, these responses can make a teenager feel that their disappointment is unreasonable. "I always believe in connection, not correction," says Dr Kohli. Instead of immediately trying to fix the situation, she suggests acknowledging the feeling and inviting the teenager to talk. Listening without judgement can help teenagers feel understood when they are disappointed by a friend's achievement or their own results. Photograph: ( iStock ) A parent could say, "I can see that this really upset you. Tell me what is bothering you the most." They could also acknowledge the specific disappointment: "Seeing someone else get something you really wanted can hurt." This gives teenagers room to express their feelings without being judged. Parents can then ask what it is about the other person's situation that they wish they had. The answer may reveal a desire for acceptance, anxiety about falling behind or uncertainty about their abilities. Once they understand the concern, parents can help their children work through it rather than dismissing it with general reassurances. Help teenagers recognise their own progress Moving away from comparison does not mean discouraging ambition. It means helping teenagers set goals based on their own needs and growth rather than someone else's achievements. Dr Kohli recommends encouraging children to measure progress against their previous efforts. Instead of asking, "Who scored higher?", parents can ask, "What was difficult for you last time, and what feels easier now?" They can also help teenagers identify skills or habits they want to improve because they matter personally, not simply because a classmate is better at them. For a student struggling with mathematics, for instance, progress might mean understanding a difficult concept or becoming more consistent with practice, even without topping the class. Recognising qualities such as kindness, curiosity and resilience can help teenagers build confidence beyond academic performance. Photograph: ( iStock ) Parents can reinforce this approach by recognising qualities beyond academic performance, including kindness, curiosity, honesty, resilience and the willingness to try again. Giving teenagers opportunities to make decisions, solve problems and contribute at home can also help them build confidence in their abilities. The example parents set matters, too. Teenagers observe how adults evaluate their own careers, appearances, homes and achievements. If comparison is a regular feature of family conversations, children may begin to see it as the natural way to measure success. "Parents don't have to model perfection," Dr Kohli says. A parent who acknowledges comparing themselves with others and explains why they are trying to focus on what matters to them can demonstrate how to recognise and manage the habit. Helping teenagers navigate social media For today's teenagers, comparisons do not end when the school day does. Social media offers a constant stream of other people's achievements, appearances, friendships and lifestyles. Dr Kohli notes that social media does not necessarily create every insecurity, but it can amplify existing ones. Teenagers may end up comparing their everyday experiences with carefully selected glimpses of other people's lives. A complete ban is not always the best solution, she says, because social media is also part of a teenager's social world. Parents can help them identify accounts that leave them feeling inadequate, curate their feeds, and take breaks when they notice these feelings intensifying. If social media is contributing to significant emotional distress, reducing exposure may be appropriate. The aim is to help teenagers become more aware of how online interactions affect them and make healthier choices about their use. Knowing when to seek professional help If comparison becomes persistent and begins affecting daily functioning, parents should consider seeking professional support. Dr Kohli highlights signs such as persistent low mood or anxiety, significant withdrawal, changes in sleep or eating habits, school refusal, loss of interest, hopelessness, self-harm or a strong sense of worthlessness. Social media can intensify feelings of inadequacy, making it important for teenagers to recognise how online content affects their self-esteem. Photograph: ( iStock ) Parents do not need to wait until these difficulties become severe before reaching out for help. Early support can help address distress before unhealthy patterns become deeply established. At home, it also helps to make room for conversations that have nothing to do with performance. Teenagers need to know their parents are interested in their thoughts, relationships and interests, not just their results. Parents can celebrate another child's achievement without turning it into a lesson for their own child. As Dr Kohli puts it, "Someone else's success does not need to become evidence of your child's failure." For a teenager who feels everyone else is moving ahead, the answer is not necessarily another reminder to work harder or think positively. It may begin with listening, understanding what feels difficult and making space for a more personal definition of progress. They do not have to be ahead of everyone else to be doing well. They need the freedom to discover what matters to them and the confidence to keep growing at their own pace.
