items.titleOriginal: Gen Z Communicates Differently in the Workplace, but Older Colleagues Can Still Decode Them
items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τον Jeff LeBlanc, έναν διαμεσολαβητή μάθησης για διαδικτυακό μεταπτυχιακό στη διοίκηση επιχειρήσεων στο Πανεπιστήμιο της Βοστώνης, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons. Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Για όλη τη συζήτηση για τη γεννήτρια…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Jeff LeBlanc , a learning facilitator for online master of business administration at Boston University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . For all the talk about generational differences at work, some of the biggest differences show up in surprisingly ordinary moments. Take being late for work. A Gen Z employee in her 20s I spoke with works at a small, locally owned café and restaurant run by an older Gen X owner. When she realized she was going to be late one day, she texted him. He was frustrated. To him, being late was serious enough to warrant a phone call, and a text felt too casual and impersonal. She saw the exact same interaction very differently. “He’s super busy, so I felt a call was going to take up too much time,” she told me. “So I texted. I thought it was more considerate.” Both thought they understood what respectful workplace communication looked like. They just had completely different definitions of it. I study workplace culture and communication, and I see this type of misunderstanding as increasingly common in multigenerational workplaces. And this is becoming more pronounced as Gen Z moves further into the workforce. The oldest members of Gen Z are now approaching 30, while the youngest are in college and high school. What’s distinctive about the older members of Gen Z is that many went through college, internships or their first jobs during the COVID-19 pandemic , when much of our communication moved online and masks often covered half our faces. And there’s a new twist now, as artificial intelligence changes how we communicate all over again. The result isn’t necessarily that Gen Z employees communicate better or worse with their bosses and colleagues than previous generations did. I argue that they have simply learned to do so in a very different environment. When a Text Means Something More The café example is an easy one to dismiss as younger workers preferring texting and feeling that phone calls are for important occasions only. But that misses what I think is the more interesting point: The employee wasn’t trying to avoid her boss. She thought she was respecting his time. For her boss, by contrast, the phone call itself carried meaning. It communicated that she understood the seriousness of being late. Neither one had explained that expectation to the other. Managers shouldn’t assume employees attach the same meaning they do to a particular form of communication. If being late requires a phone call, they need to say so. A two-minute conversation about expectations can prevent both people from walking away from an interaction believing the other was disrespectful. Another common stumble concerns openness, which might feel like oversharing. One Gen Z worker I spoke with had recently started a job at a large New England company in a blue-collar industry. He was struggling with severe anxiety and decided to tell his baby boomer manager. The manager was sympathetic, but also uneasy. “It made me feel uncomfortable, if I’m being honest,” the manager told me. “I didn’t want to downplay his anxiety, but I’m not sure I needed to know.” That distinction matters. His reaction wasn’t that anxiety wasn’t real or that his employee should simply get over it. But he questioned how much of it belonged in their professional relationship. Many older workers learned that professionalism is about setting clear boundaries between personal and professional life. Members of Gen Z are coming of age during a period when conversations about mental health and personal well-being are considerably more public. What feels like honesty to one person can feel like oversharing to their boss. This doesn’t mean that managers have to become therapists, and employees don’t have to disclose everything happening in their lives. But both may need to recognize that their comfort level around disclosure isn’t universal. Aleksandra Sapozhnikova on Unsplash, CC BY What younger workers may see as honesty could be seen as oversharing by older colleagues, who tend to keep more boundaries over personal information. Learning to Read a Room When the Room Disappeared Some workplace communication is never spoken at all. Think about how people traditionally learned to read a room. They watched faces around a conference table. They noticed a change in a manager’s tone. Someone caught them after a meeting and quietly explained what had just happened. Now think about someone who was 18 or 19 in 2020. At exactly the age when many young people would have been developing these skills in college, internships and early jobs, the room disappeared. Classes went online. Internships became remote. When people returned in person, masks sometimes made facial communication more difficult. That doesn’t mean members of Gen Z can’t read facial expressions, but we should be careful about assuming everyone had the same opportunities to learn the unwritten signals of professional life. If feedback matters, I believe managers should say it. A disappointed expression on a Zoom call is a poor substitute for a conversation. I Thought That Was Understood Imagine a manager telling a young employee: “I need this by Friday.” The employee sends it back at 4:30 p.m. that Friday afternoon. The manager is annoyed because they intended to review it that morning, make changes and send it along to someone else. The employee is equally confused. The deadline was Friday, and they met it. This deadline mismatch gets at something I have repeatedly encountered in my research with Gen Z workers. In a survey I conducted of 250 Gen Z professionals across industries, clear structural expectations emerged alongside fairness and empathetic engagement as recurring themes. If an employee wants clarity , it shouldn’t automatically be confused with hand-holding. An employee can want autonomy and still want to know exactly what success looks like. “Friday” and “Friday by 10 a.m. because I need three hours to review this” communicate very different expectations. Artificial intelligence may make this issue even more important. We can now produce polished emails, summarize meetings and generate information faster than ever. But more communication does not guarantee more understanding. I believe that may be the larger lesson for every generation working together. We tend to mistake the workplace norms we learned for common sense. They aren’t. They were taught to us by the workplaces, technologies and moments in history in which we began our careers. Gen Z is learning theirs in a very different world. RELATED: In New Book, Therapist Defines 5 Communication Types — Here’s Why It Helps to Know Yours

items.descriptionOriginal: A surprising discovery at UC San Diego suggests that chronic lower back pain may become deeply embedded in the brain's sense of personal identity. Researchers found that movement-triggered pain activates a brain network associated with self-awareness and memories, even though ordinary acute pain typically shuts this network down. This unexpected difference could explain why conventional pain medications often provide limited relief and why fear, anticipation, and past experiences can intensify chronic pain.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A new analysis by energy think tank Ember finds that six European countries collectively avoided close to $2.2 billion (approximately €2 billion) in oil import costs between March and August 2026. The savings came directly from EV fleets reducing how much oil those countries needed to import. Those numbers land differently now that oil prices have climbed 33 percent since the Iran conflict began in late February 2026. Brent crude traded near $100 a barrel in late October, up from $67 before hostilities started. Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz, a 104-mile (167-kilometer) shipping channel carrying about one-fifth of the world’s daily oil and liquefied natural gas supply, has been the main reason why. Europe’s share of a $20 billion shift Globally, the EV boom displaced an estimated 200 million barrels of crude oil, worth around $20 billion, over those six months. China accounts for the largest share: its fleet of roughly 44 million EVs saved $14 billion in oil costs. EU member states accounted for another $3.1 billion. Within Europe, Germany and France led on raw savings, at around $760 million and $560 million respectively. Denmark’s numbers told a different story. Its EV fleet displaced 6.4 million barrels of oil per year as of August 2026, equal to 13 percent of the country’s entire 2025 oil consumption, the highest share in Europe. The UK displaced around $790 million in crude over the six months; the country imported roughly $27 billion (approximately £21.5 billion) worth of crude in the preceding year. The security dividend Global EV sales grew 11 percent year-on-year in the first eight months of 2026, while combustion engine vehicle sales fell six percent. “The countries that invested in EVs before this crisis are now better protected,” said Euan Graham, a senior energy analyst at Ember, “and a growing number are following.” An EV doesn’t run on oil. At national scale, that translates to real insulation from price shocks driven by conflict or supply disruptions. “Every EV on the road reduces exposure to volatile oil markets,” Graham said, “and as fleets grow, so does the protection against future supply shocks.” The countries that invested in EVs before oil prices climbed now have a specific dollar figure for what that looked like. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Not every vegetable belongs in a backyard garden. Some take up space, demand attention, and still cost more to grow than to buy once you factor in seeds, soil, and the time it takes. But some crops genuinely save you money, and if your grocery bill has been creeping up, those are the ones to plant. Robert Westerfield , a horticulture specialist at the University of Georgia , and Damon Abdi , assistant professor at the Louisiana State University AgCente r, both weigh in on what pays off at home. Seven vegetables made the list. Herbs Westerfield describes herbs as “so forgiving,” and the economics back that up. Fresh herbs are among the most expensive produce per ounce at the grocery store, and a purchased bunch often goes partly to waste before you get through it. A plant in your garden means you take what you need, when you need it, and nothing wilts in the back of the drawer. Rosemary is an especially smart first choice. It’s evergreen, drought-tolerant, and flowers in a way that looks good in the garden, not just the kitchen. Abdi recommends it specifically because you can harvest on demand rather than buying packaged herbs that “can languish if left unused.” Peppers Peppers are resilient in a way that a lot of vegetables aren’t. Westerfield calls them cold-hardy and says they “come through disease and insects better than anything.” They need consistent water and well-draining soil, but they produce over a long season, and fresh peppers aren’t cheap. Tomatoes Cherry tomatoes are the easiest entry point. Westerfield recommends starting with one or two plants, which he says will supply you through the season with “less trouble than the larger ones.” Give them a trellis or something to climb and they’ll mostly look after themselves. Green beans Green beans can be seeded directly into the ground, no transplants needed, and they produce heavily once they get going. “If you take care of them, you can harvest into the summer,” Westerfield says. They’re a forgiving crop and a reliable one, which makes them a sensible place to start. Asparagus Asparagus is a different kind of investment. Both Westerfield and Abdi recommend it, but the payoff takes patience. The first year or two are about establishment. By the third and fourth year, the harvest grows. A well-maintained bed can produce for up to 20 years. “Asparagus is pricey up front and takes a little time and effort, but it’s perennial once you get it established,” Westerfield says. “You’ll have it basically for life. They can keep on loving you as long as you love them.” Abdi notes that asparagus does best where winters are cool, and that gardeners in warmer climates should look for cold-hardy varieties bred for those conditions. Cucumbers Cucumbers produce heavily and pickle well, so a good summer harvest can stretch well into winter with a few jars on the shelf. Keep them off the ground by growing vertically, and they’ll stay healthier through the season. Squash Squash is easy to grow, though squash bugs and squash vine borers can derail a season quickly if you let them get ahead of you. Stay on top of those two pests, and you’ll come away with a solid harvest. One honest caveat Westerfield is all in on home growing, but he’s clear-eyed about the work involved. It takes time, effort, and real upfront cost. “You know what you put on it and you know where it comes from,” he says. “Usually, the taste and quality are outstanding. There’s nothing quite like fresh tomatoes and sweet corn out of the garden.” The garden only saves money if you’re harvesting and eating what you planted, so starting with the vegetables your household already goes through most is how you make sure it does. items.descriptionOriginal: Millennials have never shied away from sharing their feelings about their Boomer parents (and their grandparenting abilities ) on the Internet. Millennials are once again uniting to discuss a similar observation about their Boomer parents’ frustrating phone use. In a July 2025 thread about generational differences on the r/generationology subreddit, Millennial member Old-Beautiful-3971 shared their frustrating experience with their Boomer parents who are perpetually on their phones. “My parents are on the very young end of being ‘boomers’. For some reason they’re both acting like me when I was 20… that is to say, gluuuued to their phones,” they wrote. “I tried to have an important conversation with my dad this morning and he did not once look up (and I’m certain he was scrolling through Instagram videos).” An older man using a cellphone. Photo credit: Canva They went on to add, “The only difference is that when I was 20 he could, and would often say ‘Look at me when I’m talking to you. Put that thing away.’ But if I said that to him now he’d get defensive and probably yell at me for being disrespectful. What the heck???” Fellow Millennials agreed The passionate post got a rousing response from fellow Millennials who have experienced the same thing with their Boomer parents. “I have noticed it too and it makes me feel even weirder for having developed in the habit of flipping my phone face-down with my hands folded on top of it to let the person know that I’m listening for that they have my attention,” one commented. “And to think that it’s coming from the generation that tells everybody else that phones and TV will rot your brains.” Another shared, “My parents are visiting me right now. My dad is glued to his phone, even at the table during meals. Never once participating in the conversation except to point at the salt. This is the same man who would have screamed at me for bringing a book to the dinner table.” Others could commiserate about the role-reversal. “I’ve noticed this with my parents. It seems like I’ve switched places with them. I’m trying to use the online world less where as they are using it more and more,” one commented. A man looking pensive with phone in hand. Photo credit: Canva When phones take over family time Some Millennials noted that their Boomer parents’ phone use has impacted other activities they attempt to do together. “It’s become so difficult to watch a movie with my parents. I tell them to put away their phone. Sometimes movies take two days to finish,” another shared. Many Millennials also shared how they communicate with their parents when they notice it. “I am witnessing that as well, my boomer mom and my almost gen z brother visit and they are both glued to their phones. I try and ask if they can put them away because I don’t like my little son to see people like that. I do scroll but never when I am with him,” one Millennial shared. Researchers have a name for this: “phubbing,” or phone snubbing, which a 2016 study linked to lower relationship satisfaction among romantic partners. A related term, “technoference,” describes how parents’ device use interrupts family time, and research on parents has tied it to more behavior problems in children over time. Another added, “I stopped visiting my boomer mom for awhile. I told her to her face that I couldn’t stand the fact that I took the time to drive to her, which I really hate driving, it scares me and I’m not very good at it, and spend MY time with her only for her to be on her phone most of that time. I stopped calling her too because of all the times she’d put me on hold to take another call and then tell me that she’d have to call me back, but she never did. I still rarely call her. I just text so it’s less intrusive and hurtful for me. Now when I visit, her and her husband stay off their phones. They turn the TV down and only put quiet music on instead of blaring whatever crap they were watching. I did thank them for it.” Gen X isn’t off the hook either However, a Gen Z commenter was quick to point out that Gen X is guilty of the same habit. “My gen x parents are hella addicted to their phones (I’m 22 for context),” they wrote. “I’m not saying i’m not, but it’s really hypocritical when they’ll be bitching at me about ‘playing on my phone too much’ when they’re literal ipad kids lol. the reality is, screens and social media are addicting to ANYONE, regardless of age.” Other Millennials pointed out that it’s not just certain generations that are addicted to their phones. “I’m guilty of it as well. Everyone is at risk of screen addiction in this era,” another noted. And another Millennial quipped, “Phones are addictive, that doesn’t just like go away with oldness.” The data suggests they have a point: Pew Research Center’s 2025 survey found that 63% of adults ages 18 to 29 say they use the internet “almost constantly,” compared with 33% of those ages 50 to 64 and 14% of those 65 and older, even though 90% of adults 50 to 64 now own a smartphone. What’s with Boomers and their phones lately? by u/Old-Beautiful-3971 in generationology Phones are tough on every generation If there’s a takeaway from this thread, it’s that the phone gap is smaller than it feels. Millennials remember being told to put the screen away, and now some are watching their parents do the very thing they were scolded for. But as plenty of commenters pointed out, nobody is immune. Whether you’re 22 or 62, a phone is built to hold your attention. Maybe the real fix isn’t pointing fingers across generations, but doing what the commenter with the quiet TV and the put-away phones did: just say something, and see what happens. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Millennials are growing concerned about their Boomer parents being glued to their phones appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Renewable Natural Gas Is Turning Everyday Waste Into Cleaner Fuel for Businesses Reading Time: 3 minutes Renewable Natural Gas Is Turning Everyday Waste Into Cleaner Fuel for Businesses The shift towards sustainability has led to numerous innovations in the way that companies operate. One of the most exciting developments is the use of renewable natural gas (RNG). RNG is created by capturing methane from sources such as agricultural runoff, landfills, and wastewater treatment plants. This not only reduces the amount of greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere but also creates a new source of energy for those facilities. Adding RNG to your natural gas procurement for businesses is a straightforward way to hit green targets without risking downtime. It tackles organic waste head-on and acts as an easy, drop-in replacement for fossil fuels. How Everyday Waste Transforms into Power The journey from refuse to resource is a fascinating one that involves the capture and processing of methane gas from decomposing organic matter before it escapes into the atmosphere. Instead of allowing this potent greenhouse gas to contribute to climate change, facilities that use anaerobic digesters are able to break down dairy manure, food scraps, and wastewater sludge. The biogas that is produced from these facilities undergoes a purification process to remove moisture, carbon dioxide, and other elements from the gas. The resulting gas is structurally identical to natural gas, allowing it to be injected into existing gas infrastructure and utilized by commercial fleets and manufacturing plants without any need for modification to their equipment. Evaluating the Financial and Environmental Dual Benefits Shifting to this circular energy model offers companies a unique opportunity to tackle two major corporate objectives simultaneously: minimizing ecological impact and stabilizing operational costs. Because RNG is domestically produced from continuous waste streams, it can help shield commercial consumers from the extreme price volatility often associated with global fossil fuel markets. When executives sit down to analyze their overall natural gas procurement strategies, incorporating a renewable component proves highly advantageous for long-term budget forecasting. Furthermore, utilizing this upgraded biogas significantly lowers a company’s direct carbon footprint, allowing brands to authentically market their sustainability achievements to an increasingly eco-conscious consumer base. Overcoming Adoption Barriers and Infrastructure Myths One of the most common misconceptions about the implementation of alternative fuels is that companies will have to invest millions of dollars into new machinery and infrastructure. However, since the upgraded biomethane is chemically identical to the geological methane that now fuels the majority of the nation’s cities and industries, the fuel can be easily implemented into the existing pipeline system without any need for the implementation of new machinery or infrastructure. Also, since the fuel is chemically identical to the existing fuel, the implementation of this new fuel source will not require the implementation of new infrastructure. Instead, the companies can simply update their purchasing agreements with the companies that produce the fuel to implement the new fuel source into their operations. Strategic Sourcing for Corporate Sustainability Goals A sophisticated strategy is needed to source sustainable energy, especially given the growing demand for environmentally friendly substitutes in a number of heavy industries. To make sure they are obtaining genuine environmental attributes in addition to their physical fuel supply, corporate buyers must negotiate a complicated web of producers, marketers, and local utility regulations. When handling natural gas procurement for businesses, look for suppliers who can trace their biomethane straight from the farm or landfill to your facility. Securing these transparent contracts makes it much easier to prove emission cuts to stakeholders and meet strict climate regulations. Embracing the Circular Economy of Tomorrow Another way in which the use of upgraded biogas can benefit commercial enterprises is in reducing their reliance on traditional fossil fuels. The use of biogas as a fuel source for these companies can help to significantly reduce their carbon footprint without any changes to their daily operations. As the technology to capture and refine methane improves, the availability and affordability of biogas will continue to increase. Companies that incorporate biogas into their energy portfolios will be at an advantage compared to their competitors who do not take such steps towards sustainability. The post Renewable Natural Gas Is Turning Everyday Waste Into Cleaner Fuel for Businesses appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: They see Vikrant Massey’s niece. But her mother sees a dancer building her own identity, one beat at a time. :sparkles: Naaz has Down syndrome, but she refuses to let other people’s expectations define her story. Where others see limitations, she finds rhythm. Where doors remain closed, she keeps creating her own stage. Through dance, awards and every opportunity to perform, she continues to show the world what she is capable of. And her biggest dream? To see her own face on a billboard. Naaz isn’t here to be known only as someone’s niece. She is here to be recognised as Naaz: a dancer, a dreamer and a young woman creating a name for herself. Her journey is a reminder that every person deserves the chance to be seen for their own talent, ambition and individuality. Her dreams deserve the spotlight, and her identity deserves to shine. items.descriptionOriginal: Compostable plastics are touted as a greener alternative to conventional petroleum-based plastics that can linger in the environment for centuries. But there’s a catch. Degradable plastics only break down in the right conditions typically found in a composting facility. The tons of compostable plastic that ends up in oceans can still float around for decades and threaten marine life and ecosystems. Researchers have found a way for plastics to break down much faster in the ocean. They embedded tiny amounts of plastic-degrading enzymes in compostable polyester plastics. The enzyme-containing polyesters completely degraded in a relatively short time period even in microbe-scarce environments. The method works at all depths from coastal waters to the deep open sea, the researchers report in the journal Nature . There are many types of biodegradable plastics in commercial use today. These plastics are designed to decompose completely by microorganisms at certain temperatures and humidities . Those conditions are found in industrial composting facilities and with more care in backyard compost settings. But out in cold ocean water, biodegradable plastics can persist for a long time. The research team from Japan took four types of compostable plastic—PBS, PBSA, PCL, and PBAT—and melted them. The heat of the melt would destroy plastic-degrading enzymes . So the researchers made freeze-dried forms of Candida antarctica lipase B and Humicola insolens cutinase enzymes. After sealing the samples in a polyethylene meshes, they placed the meshes at various locations off the coast of Tokyo, ranging in water depths from 2–6 m to 5,503 m. They monitored the samples over periods ranging from one month to 18 months. At 757 m, PBS, PBSA and PCL films containing 3% cutinase nearly completely disappeared within five months. items.descriptionOriginal: On a polluted day, the air can look like a grey haze hanging over a city, obscuring buildings and making every breath feel heavier. But what if some of that pollution could be collected, transformed and given a new purpose — not as waste, but as a material used to build our homes and workplaces? Mumbai-based architect Tejas Sidnal is exploring precisely that possibility. Through his startup, Carbon Craft Design, he is turning recovered black carbon into architectural tiles, giving a second life to a pollutant while rethinking how building materials are made. The idea took shape when Sidnal, while studying architecture, became fascinated by biomimicry — the practice of drawing inspiration from nature to solve human problems. He began questioning what truly makes a society healthy, looking beyond grand buildings to the essentials of clean air, water and food. The startup combines recovered carbon with cement, recycled marble powder and marble chips to create its signature Carbon Tiles. Photograph: ( Architecture + Desig n) This led him to a contradiction: the construction industry itself contributes significantly to global carbon emissions, yet the materials used to create our built environment are rarely viewed through the lens of pollution. Could the very carbon waste contributing to the problem become part of the solution? In 2020, Sidnal launched Carbon Craft Design to turn this question into a tangible innovation: Carbon Tiles. How does carbon waste become a tile? Black carbon is produced by the incomplete combustion of fuels and other carbon-rich materials. When released into the atmosphere, it contributes to air pollution and climate change. Carbon Craft Design sources recovered carbon waste from industrial processes, including tyre recycling and factory pyrolysis . The material is cleaned and processed before being blended with cement, recycled marble powder and marble chips. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Anuj Mohanty (@anujmohanty_) The mixture is then compressed using hydraulic presses to create tiles with distinctive geometric patterns. Unlike conventional ceramic tiles, which typically require energy-intensive firing in high-temperature kilns, Carbon Tiles are compressed and allowed to set at room temperature. According to the startup, this manufacturing process uses around one-fifth of the energy required to make conventional fired tiles. The company also states that every square metre of its tiles prevents the equivalent of 25 kg of carbon dioxide emissions. Made using hydraulic presses and set at room temperature, Carbon Tiles avoid the energy-intensive firing process used for conventional ceramic tiles. Photograph: ( Wallparer ) By incorporating recovered carbon into a durable building material, the startup aims to give waste a useful destination instead of allowing it to contribute to the pollution burden. A little science, a little craft & a lot of creativity For Sidnal, sustainability is not just about developing a new material. It is also about rethinking how products are made and who gets to make them. Carbon Craft Design collaborates with ceramic artisans in Morbi, Gujarat, a region known for its tile-making industry. Drawing on traditional craftsmanship, the artisans handcraft the tiles' distinctive geometric patterns, bringing character and detail to the material. Carbon Craft Design collaborates with ceramic artisans in Morbi, Gujarat, to create geometric tile patterns that combine traditional craftsmanship with material innovation. Photograph: ( Carbon Craft Design ) This partnership brings together material research and established craft skills. The recovered carbon and low-energy manufacturing process address environmental concerns, while the artisans' expertise helps create tiles suited to contemporary architectural spaces. The result is a product that places sustainability alongside aesthetics — an important consideration in an industry where materials must be functional as well as visually appealing. From an architect's ideas to showrooms Turning an environmental concept into a commercially viable product requires more than a promising material. It needs customers willing to use it, too. Carbon Craft Design has worked with major brands, including Adidas, creating tile patterns for its showrooms. Such projects demonstrate how recycled materials can find a place in commercial interiors, where design and durability matter alongside sustainability. Carbon Craft Design has created custom tile patterns for Adidas showrooms, bringing recycled materials into commercial spaces. Photograph: ( Carbon Craft Design ) The startup has also received support from impact investors, including Social Alpha and the Pilani Innovation Entrepreneurship Development Society, and participated in climate-focused accelerators. Its recognitions include the Lexus Design Award India in 2020 and the No Waste Challenge, organised by What Design Can Do and the IKEA Foundation, in 2021. These milestones reflect a growing interest in materials that rethink the traditional journey from resource extraction to manufacturing and disposal. Could the buildings of tomorrow be made from today's waste? No single material can solve the climate crisis. Construction must continue to address emissions across its supply chains, energy use and building lifecycles, while innovations such as Carbon Tiles must demonstrate their durability, safety and environmental benefits at scale. But Sidnal's work offers a tangible starting point. By recovering carbon waste, reducing the energy used in tile manufacturing and working with traditional artisans, Carbon Craft Design brings together pollution management, sustainable production and local craftsmanship. Carbon Craft Design shows how recovered carbon waste can be transformed into durable building materials, rethinking how the spaces we inhabit are made. Photograph: ( Carbon Craft Design ) The idea is both simple and powerful: something that once contributed to an environmental problem can become part of the spaces people inhabit every day. And perhaps that is where a cleaner future begins — not only by preventing waste, but by learning to see its potential before it is discarded. Sources: 'Tejas Jindal' by Indian Diaspora 'Tejas Sidnal' by What Design Can Do Carbon Craft Design

items.descriptionOriginal: Cranberry juice may offer an unexpected benefit beyond its reputation for helping prevent urinary tract infections: protecting teeth from decay. Researchers at the University of Illinois Chicago discovered that pure, unsweetened cranberry juice slowed the regrowth of dental plaque bacteria and reduced their production of acids that damage tooth enamel. The secret may lie in naturally occurring compounds called proanthocyanidins, which interfere with harmful bacteria.

items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine having to walk more than a kilometre every time you need to bring home drinking water. On a hot summer day, even filling a few pots can mean a tiring journey, with no guarantee that there will be enough water for everyone at home. For years, this was a reality for families in Wadji, a village in Maharashtra's Washim district. Residents travelled up to 1.5 km to fetch drinking water, a struggle made harder during the summer months when water sources became scarce. But what if the answer to their water problem was all around them, quite literally, in the air they breathe? That is the idea behind Meghdoot, a machine that draws moisture from the air and turns it into drinking water. Installed in Wadji, the technology can produce up to 500 litres of purified water a day, offering the village a new source of water without having to rely entirely on wells or groundwater. Even a pot of drinking water meant a long walk Wadji, home to nearly 2,000 people, is among the communities in Vidarbha grappling with water scarcity. The challenge extends beyond the village. According to Central Ground Water Board reports, nearly 40 villages in Risod taluka fall under the semi-critical groundwater category. For years, residents of Wadji village in Maharashtra walked up to 1.5 km to fetch drinking water. Photograph: ( Frontline ) For residents, the problem becomes particularly difficult during summer, when temperatures rise, and reliable access to drinking water becomes harder to secure. To address this, the Wadji Gram Panchayat adopted a technology that draws on a resource people rarely think of as a source of drinking water: the moisture present in the air. The village is reported to be the first and only one in Maharashtra to have adopted this technology. How does the technology turn air into water? The system, called Meghdoot, uses Atmospheric Water Generation technology to extract moisture from the air and convert it into liquid water. The process begins with fans drawing humid air into the machine. Filters remove airborne particles such as dust and pollen before a refrigeration-based mechanism cools the air to its dew point. As the air cools, water vapour condenses into droplets, much like moisture forming on the outside of a cold glass. Developed by CSIR-IICT scientists in Hyderabad in collaboration with Maithri Aquatech, Meghdoot offers an alternative source of drinking water. Photograph: ( Maithri Aquatech ) The collected water then undergoes further purification. Activated carbon filtration, ultraviolet (UV) disinfection and other treatment processes help make it suitable for drinking. The purified water is stored before being made available for consumption. The unit has a reported capacity of around 500 litres a day. However, actual output from atmospheric water generators can depend on conditions such as humidity and temperature, as well as the machine's operation. Unlike conventional sources that draw directly on groundwater or surface water, this approach collects moisture from the atmosphere. It can therefore provide an additional source of drinking water in places where existing supplies are under pressure. The Hyderabad scientists and villagers behind Wadji's water innovation The technology was developed by scientists at the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-Indian Institute of Chemical Technology (CSIR-IICT) in Hyderabad, in collaboration with Maithri Aquatech. Key contributors to the project include Dr Sridhar, Dr Nivedita Sahu and their team. The system was procured with support from CSIR-IICT under the guidance of its then director, Dr Chandrasekhar. At the village level, the Wadji Gram Panchayat took the initiative to bring the technology to the community. The unit has been installed at the Zilla Parishad Primary School and Anganwadi, making drinking water accessible at locations used by children and local residents. Installed at Wadji's Zilla Parishad Primary School and Anganwadi, the unit brings drinking water closer to children and local residents. Photograph: ( NDTV ) Its placement at these institutions also gives schoolchildren and Anganwadi attendees an opportunity to benefit from a source of drinking water close to where they spend part of their day. Could this help other villages facing water shortages? Atmospheric water generation is not a substitute for groundwater conservation, rainwater harvesting or reliable public water infrastructure. The technology also requires electricity, and its output depends on local atmospheric conditions. Its long-term usefulness will depend on operating costs, maintenance and consistent performance. By drawing moisture from the air, Meghdoot offers Wadji residents an alternative source of drinking water amid growing water scarcity. Photograph: (Outlook India) For Wadji, the promise of Meghdoot lies in something simple: bringing drinking water closer to the people who need it. What once required a journey of a kilometre or more could now be met, in part, by a machine that draws moisture from the air. While the technology cannot replace long-term solutions such as groundwater conservation and rainwater harvesting, it offers another way to address water shortages. If maintained well and adapted to local conditions, such innovations could help more communities explore alternative sources of drinking water, one village at a time. Source: 'When wells run dry, Vidarbha's Wadji literally taps drinking water from air' : by Bhaskar Mehare for The Times Of India, Published on 13 June 2026. 'Video: Drinking water from the humidity in the air! Innovative experiment by Gram Panchayat' : by Loksatta, Published on 13 June 2026.

items.descriptionOriginal: A healthy garden does not always require expensive pots, planters, or gardening equipment. Some of the things that can help plants grow may already be sitting in your kitchen or storeroom, waiting to be thrown away. From plastic bottles and old buckets to kitchen scraps and eggshells, everyday household items can find a second life in a garden. Indian gardeners are already putting these ideas into practice, turning discarded materials into growing spaces and organic compost. Here are seven ways to reuse household items in your garden, inspired by people who are doing it themselves. 1. Plastic bottles can become planters Empty plastic bottles can be turned into planters for herbs, leafy greens, and other plants that do not need much root space. Wash a bottle thoroughly, cut it to the desired size, and make drainage holes at the bottom before adding potting mix. A healthy garden does not always require expensive pots, planters, or gardening equipment. Photograph: (OneGreenPlanet) You can also arrange bottles vertically to make use of a small balcony wall. Mandeep Sangwan and students in Delhi created vertical gardens using discarded plastic bottles. Their initiative shows how waste can be turned into green spaces, even where ground space is limited. 2. Old buckets and containers can grow vegetables An unused bucket, plastic tub, or drum can provide a home for tomatoes, chillies, and leafy greens. Choose a container that is deep enough for the crop, clean it thoroughly, and make drainage holes before filling it with potting mix. Avoid containers that previously held paint, pesticides, oils, or other chemicals, especially when growing edible plants. Shivanand Hongal and students in Sirsi, Karnataka , found creative ways to reuse waste in their garden. Along with plastic bottles, they used broken buckets, cement bags, and tin cans to grow plants. Their work shows how discarded objects can become practical growing containers. 3. Coconut shells can become small planters Coconut shells are sturdy and can be used as small planters for succulents, seedlings, and other compact plants. Clean the shell, make drainage holes if possible, and fill it with a suitable potting mix. They can also add a natural touch to a balcony garden. However, their limited size makes them unsuitable for plants that need plenty of room for their roots. Sakshi Bharadwaj from Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh , has reused materials such as coconut shells and plastic bottles in her garden, which features thousands of plants. Her approach offers inspiration for gardeners who want to make use of everyday discarded objects. 4. Vegetable peels can become compost Fruit peels, vegetable scraps, and other suitable kitchen waste can be turned into compost. Instead of throwing away banana peels, carrot tops, and other uncooked scraps, collect them in a home compost bin. Mix these green materials with brown materials such as dry leaves, shredded cardboard, and uncoated paper. Keep the mixture moist but not waterlogged, and turn it occasionally to allow air to circulate. Fruit peels, vegetable scraps, and other suitable kitchen waste can be turned into compost. K Subbalakshmi from Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh , uses household wet waste to make compost for her garden. Her example shows how kitchen waste can be put to use instead of being sent to landfill. Avoid adding meat, dairy products, and oils to a basic home compost pile, as these can attract pests and create unpleasant odours. 5. Eggshells can be added to compost Eggshells contain calcium carbonate and can be added to a home compost pile. Rinse them, allow them to dry, and crush them into small pieces before mixing them with vegetable scraps and dry leaves. Crushing the shells helps them break down more readily, although decomposition can still take time. Eggshells are not an instant fertiliser, so do not rely on them alone to address a plant's nutritional needs. Evangeline Wilson from Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh , has worked to reduce household waste by composting kitchen scraps and making use of materials such as eggshells, tea leaves, and vegetable peels. 6. Used tea leaves can enrich compost After making chai , save the used tea leaves rather than throwing them away. They can be added to compost, where they contribute organic matter as they decompose. Let the leaves cool before collecting them and mix them with dry leaves, cardboard, or other brown materials. If you use tea bags, check whether they contain plastic and remove any non-compostable parts. Tea leaves can be useful compost ingredients, but they should not replace a balanced compost mix. Avoid piling large quantities directly around plant stems. Evangeline Wilson's waste-reduction efforts in Prayagraj also offer a useful example of how everyday kitchen leftovers can be diverted from the rubbish bin and put to better use. 7. Newspapers and cardboard can help suppress weeds Plain cardboard and uncoated newspapers can help cover bare soil and suppress weeds around established plants. Remove tape, staples, and plastic labels before using them. Reusing household items does not mean saving everything that might possibly be useful. Photograph: (Etsy) Lay the cardboard over the soil, leaving space around plant stems, and wet it so that it stays in place. Cover it with dry leaves or another suitable organic mulch. Shredded newspaper can also be added to compost as a source of carbon. Avoid glossy paper and cardboard contaminated with grease or chemicals. Do not pack cardboard tightly against plant stems, as this can trap moisture and encourage rot. This is another way to reduce household waste while making garden maintenance easier. If you have old packaging or newspapers, check whether they are suitable for reuse before putting them in the bin. Make the most of what you have Reusing household items does not mean saving everything that might possibly be useful. The key is to choose materials that are clean, safe, and suitable for the task. Start with one or two ideas that suit your home and the plants you already grow. A few simple changes can reduce waste while making gardening more affordable. Sometimes, the next useful addition to your garden is already waiting in your kitchen or storeroom.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Removing Forever Chemicals from Farmlands Gets Easier with New Eco-Friendly, Affordable Method Reading Time: 3 minutes A new Yale-led study finds that removing forever chemicals from farmlands could become far cheaper using hemp, rock dust, and biochar, potentially cleaning contaminated soils within a decade. Removing Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) from farmlands could soon become far cheaper and far less destructive. A new Yale-led study outlines a three-step process using plants, rock dust, and biochar. Researchers say it could work within a single decade. The chemicals in question are often called “forever chemicals.” They resist breaking down and have built up in soil for decades. Much of that contamination traces back to sewage sludge once used as fertilizer. Removing forever chemicals from farmlands matters because these chemicals do not simply fade away on their own. Once present in soil, they can persist for generations without intervention. That persistence is part of why the chemicals earned their nickname in the first place. The study estimates PFAS have contaminated roughly 1.2 million hectares of U.S. cropland. Some Maine farms have already shut down after soil tests exceeded safety limits. Exposure to these chemicals has been linked to certain cancers, thyroid problems, and fertility issues. Health researchers have also linked long-term PFAS exposure to weakened immune response. These risks make removing forever chemicals from farmland a public health priority, not just an environmental one. Farmers directly exposed to contaminated soil and water face some of the highest risks. Conventional cleanup methods of removing forever chemicals from farmlands usually means excavating and burning contaminated soil entirely. That approach can cost an estimated $1.6 million per hectare. Scaled nationally, the total bill could reach roughly $8 trillion. The Yale team’s model instead starts with basalt rock dust spread across farmland. This dust shifts soil pH in a way that sounds counterproductive at first. It actually makes PFAS more available for uptake by nearby plants. Hemp and certain perennial grasses then draw the loosened PFAS out of the soil. Rock dust sped up removal of one compound, called PFOS, by 20-40%. Researchers call PFOS the higher regulatory priority of the two chemicals studied. Harvested plants next go through a heating process to make biochar. That heat destroys much of the remaining chemical structure left in the plant tissue. Spreading the finished biochar back onto contaminated fields could cut chemical runoff by 95%. A Yale-developed process for removing forever chemicals from farmlands uses basalt rock dust to loosen chemical bonds in contaminated soil, allowing hemp (photo above) and perennial grasses to draw pollutants up through their roots before harvesting and heating the plants into biochar that, spread back onto fields, could cut PFAS runoff by 95%. Photo by Mark Stebnicki on Pexels. Postdoctoral researcher Jake Thompson led the study alongside professor Noah Planavsky at Yale. Planavsky, who comes from a farming family, says farmers urgently need better tools to address this problem. Thompson notes that small and organic farms were often hit hardest by past PFAS-laden fertilizer use. Combined, researchers project these steps could bring soils below safety thresholds within a decade. Estimated costs come in at around $1,460 per hectare each year. That figure is a tiny fraction of traditional excavation and burning costs. The rock dust and biochar processes also carry an added climate benefit. Both methods help pull carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere over time. Scaled nationwide, researchers estimate the approach could remove 10.5 million metric tons of carbon dioxide each year. Unlike excavation, this method would let farmers keep working their land throughout the process. Researchers note that removing forever chemicals from farmlands is a global issue beyond the United States. In parts of Europe and the UK, most sewage sludge still gets applied directly to farmland. Europe alone spreads about 10 million tons of sewage sludge onto cropland each year. The United Kingdom applies sludge to roughly 70% of its farmland. China follows a similar pattern, researchers say, making the contamination problem a shared one worldwide. So far, the findings come from computer modeling built on real farm data rather than full field trials. The research team now hopes to test the approach on partner farms across different soil types. Real-world results of removing forever chemicals from farmlands through this approach will show whether these modeled gains hold up outside the lab. If they do, hemp, rock dust, and biochar could offer struggling farmers a genuine way forward. For land written off as unusable, that alone would count as real progress. The post Removing Forever Chemicals from Farmlands Gets Easier with New Eco-Friendly, Affordable Method appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: What makes a museum worth travelling across the world for? In Patna, Bihar Museum has made a strong case for itself. It has been ranked ninth among the world's 100 best museums in 2026, ahead of New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art, popularly known as The Met, and Paris's Louvre. Designed by Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki, Bihar Museum brings contemporary architecture and the state's rich cultural heritage together. Photograph: (Instagram/ @just.adulting ) Worth a Journey, an independent travel guide based in Munich, Germany, compiled the ranking using visitor reviews, data analysis, and on-site assessments. Bihar Museum is the highest-ranked museum in Asia on its list and the only Indian institution to feature in the top 100. But beyond the ranking, what can visitors expect to find here? Think ancient sculptures, archaeological treasures, folk art and contemporary architecture, all coming together to tell the story of a region whose cultural legacy stretches back centuries. A modern space for Bihar's ancient stories Established in 2015, Bihar Museum was created to give the state's rich collection of historical artefacts a larger space for display. The existing Patna Museum already held a substantial collection, but a new institution offered an opportunity to present Bihar's heritage on a much larger scale. Spread across more than 13 acres, the museum was designed by Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki, in collaboration with Mumbai-based Opolis Architects. The result is a contemporary building with expansive galleries, open courtyards and landscaped spaces that make exploring the museum an experience in itself. Ancient sculptures at Bihar Museum offer a glimpse into Bihar's artistic traditions and centuries-old history. Photograph: (Instagram/ @patnaite ) Inside, the exhibits take visitors through Bihar's history, from its early civilisations to 1764. Ancient sculptures, archaeological finds, coins and manuscripts offer glimpses into the lives, beliefs and artistic traditions of people who lived here long before the modern state took shape. The museum also makes room for living traditions, with galleries dedicated to folk and contemporary art. Together, the collections tell a story that goes beyond dynasties and dates to explore how people have expressed themselves through art and culture . What makes it worth the journey? For families travelling with children, the museum has a dedicated Children's Gallery featuring subjects such as animals, folk art, culture and science. It offers younger visitors a way to engage with the exhibits beyond simply looking at objects behind glass. The Diaspora Gallery explores Bihar's connections with communities beyond the state, adding another dimension to its history. And for visitors who want to sample local flavours along the way, the museum also has a restaurant serving Bihari cuisine. Bihar Museum's folk art collections celebrate the artistic traditions that continue to shape the state's cultural identity. Photograph: ( NewsMobile ) The architecture is another reason to spend time here. The interplay of indoor galleries, open spaces and landscaped courtyards gives visitors room to pause between exhibits. Rather than treating history as a collection of artefacts to hurry past, the museum offers several ways to explore it at one's own pace. For anyone visiting Patna , it is an opportunity to discover Bihar through its art, people and past, all under one roof. The company Bihar Museum keeps Bihar Museum's ninth-place ranking puts it among some of the world's best-known cultural institutions. Mexico City's Museo Nacional de Antropolog a leads the 2026 list, followed by Madrid's Museo del Prado and Denmark's Louisiana Museum of Modern Art. Archaeological artefacts at Bihar Museum help visitors explore the region's past, from early civilisations to later historical periods. Photograph: ( Instagram/@mrincoder & @aspectrum ) Russia's State Hermitage Museum ranks fourth, while Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum takes fifth place. Turkey's Şanlıurfa Archaeology Museum is sixth, followed by Poland's Museum of the Second World War and the National WWII Museum in New Orleans, USA. The Met ranks tenth, while the Louvre is placed 31st. For its 2026 edition, Worth a Journey says it analysed more than one million venues to create 36 lists of the world's best places across travel and hospitality categories. Its museum ranking draws attention to destinations that may not always receive the same global recognition as their more famous counterparts. A reason to discover Bihar differently A museum visit can change how we see a place. A sculpture becomes a clue to an older civilisation; a piece of folk art opens a window into everyday life; and an architectural space brings centuries of history into the present. The museum's spacious galleries and open courtyards make exploring Bihar's history an experience beyond the exhibits themselves. Photograph: (Instagram/ @just.adulting ) At Bihar Museum, these stories come together in a setting that is distinctly contemporary yet deeply rooted in the region it represents. Its place among the world's top 10 offers travellers another reason to put Patna on their itinerary. More importantly, it invites them to look beyond familiar tourist destinations and discover the many layers of India's cultural heritage, one gallery at a time. Sources: 'Bihar Museum is Asia's highest-ranked museum on World's 100 Best Museums 2026 list' by Firstpost, Published on 28 October 2026. items.description: Το 1991, η Saskia Sassen δημοσίευσε την Παγκόσμια Πόλη στην οποία υποστήριξε ότι το Λονδίνο είχε περισσότερα κοινά με τη Νέα Υόρκη και το Τόκιο παρά με άλλα μέρη του Ηνωμένου Βασιλείου. Th…
items.descriptionOriginal: I n 1991, Saskia Sassen published The Global City in which she asserted that London had more in common with New York and Tokyo than it did with other parts of the U.K. The geography of culture wasn’t delineated by national borders, she argued — there was no need to travel across an ocean to experience ways of life vastly different from your own. That ethos is embodied by American Exchange Project, an intercultural exchange program for youth that takes place entirely within the United States. The exchanges send students who have just graduated high school on weeklong sojourns to U.S. communities completely different from their own. Participating students then host a cohort of peers in their own town, creating a true interchange of American experiences. For many of these students, the exchange is not only an opportunity to see a different part of the country, but to have deep discussions with their new friends about how their lives are different — and the same. “I hadn’t really experienced something where the point of spending time together was to talk about this big, deep stuff,” says Alden Swanson, a student from Chestertown, Maryland whose exchange took place in Orem, Utah. “And that led to so many interesting conversations about differences, but also brought up a lot of similarities about beliefs and how we thought about the world.” Interactions like these are becoming rarer, as Americans increasingly choose to live in cities and towns where their neighbors hold views similar to their own. According to Bill Bishop, author of The Big Sort: Why the Clustering of Like-Minded America Is Tearing Us Apart , the share of voters living in “landslide counties” — where a presidential candidate won by 20 or more points — rose from about 26 percent in 1976 to more than 60 percent in 2016. People are proactively moving to communities with less political and cultural heterogeneity. More than two out of five Americans consider it important that their neighbors share their politics, according to Bishop. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] That said, American Exchange Project makes it clear that these exchanges aren’t about exposing students to new political views (any more than a foreign exchange program would primarily be about politics). Instead, they’re a rare opportunity to immerse young people in an unfamiliar American context and help them build empathy for those whose communities and cultures diverge from their own. Sunny Beam, a student from Ilwaco, Washington, had never spent time in a place with a population of more than 10,000 people before her exchange sent her to the Bronx in New York City. “It’s not even comparable to the places I lived before. It was so nice,” she says. “You’d think that living in a small town, everyone’s super closely knit together, but that’s not always a good thing.” The culture shock of being transported from small town to booming metropolis was offset by the hospitality she was shown by a city used to embracing people of all stripes. Alden Swanson and some of her American Exchange Project peers. Courtesy of Alden Swanson “Because everyone didn’t know everyone else, you would think that they’d be super-standoffish, but everyone was just incredibly welcoming, even to strangers,” she says. “It felt more community-based than my town because everyone was so welcoming and everyone was so willing to, like, work with the diversity rather than shut people out.” For Andrew Wood from Kilgore, Texas, who was also sent to New York, one of the biggest lessons of the exchange was that connecting across cultures needn’t be complicated. “I’m a person who likes to bring the group together,” says Wood. “And so as soon as we got there, I’m like, ‘Okay, guys, you want to play some UNO? Because they got UNO cards for us.’ And so we decided to play UNO, and we started talking and getting to know each other, and we kind of just really clicked from there.” The post The Student Exchange Program That Never Leaves the U.S. appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Study Reveals Primates Forming Cross-Species Friendships with Dogs, Deer, and Pigs Worldwide Reading Time: 3 minutes An international review documents 427 cases of primates forming cross-species friendships. Why do humans keep pets? A new study led by researchers at the University of Oxford and collaborators worldwide suggests the behavioral foundations of human-animal companionship may not be unique to humans. The team compiled the first comprehensive review of friendly interactions between nonhuman primates and other species, documenting 427 cases involving 88 primate species and 127 partner species, 55 of them non-primates. Published in the journal Primates, the study draws together evidence spanning several decades, from the 1970s through 2025, combining 303 cases from scientific literature, 58 cases from screened photographs and videos, and 66 cases collected through a global survey of primatologists. Together, these sources produced 204 distinct species pairings, making this the most comprehensive overview to date of cross-species social behavior among monkeys and apes. The diversity documented among primates forming cross-species friendships proved remarkable. Partner species included sheep, tapirs, deer, domestic pigs, cats, and dogs, as well as owls, lizards, toads, and even insects. Play and grooming emerged as the most common behaviors, recorded in 139 and 136 cases, respectively, but researchers also found primates carrying, huddling, sharing food with, and occasionally adopting individuals from entirely different species. One of the most striking and now well-documented examples of primates forming cross-species friendships involves Japanese macaques in Yakushima, Japan, who groom and ride on the backs of sika deer, repeatedly interacting peacefully over long periods. In China’s Yunnan Golden Monkey National Park, researchers observed a young black-and-white snub-nosed monkey playing on the back of a domestic pig. Elsewhere, a langur was seen attentively stroking a squirrel, a silverback gorilla carefully cradled a tiny wild bushbaby, and a bonobo gently held a mongoose pup. Domestic dogs appeared repeatedly throughout the review, with researchers recording 26 wild or free-ranging encounters involving dogs. Rhesus macaques and dogs formed one of the most frequently reported species pairings in the entire dataset, suggesting these interactions represent more than isolated curiosities. Most interactions among primates forming cross-species friendships occurred between closely related species with similar bodies, gestures, and social habits, animals that may find it easier to interpret one another without conflict. Yet evolutionary distance proved far from an insurmountable barrier. Age and sex patterns emerged clearly across the dataset: juvenile and infant monkeys were significantly more likely to initiate play than grooming, while adult females showed the opposite pattern, favoring grooming behaviors instead. Researchers suggest play may offer young primates a flexible, low-stakes way to test an unfamiliar partner’s temperament. A chase, a leap, or a playful climb can quickly reveal whether another animal responds with tolerance, enthusiasm, or aggression, information valuable before investing in a longer social bond. Notably, unlike many mixed-species groupings found in nature, these friendships did not appear to provide obvious survival advantages such as improved access to food or protection from predators. Instead, the animals frequently played together, groomed one another, carried each other, or simply rested side by side, behaviors suggesting that primates forming cross-species friendships reflect genuine curiosity and social flexibility extending well beyond mere practical necessity. Primates forming cross-species friendships suggest curiosity and social flexibility rather than a survival advantage, with juveniles more likely to initiate play while adult females favored grooming behaviors instead. Photos by (a) Nicholas Chapoy, (b) Sabit Hasan, (c) Senthi Aathavan Senthilverl, and (d) Neil Challis, courtesy of Primates . Not every interaction ended positively. Curiosity and caregiving occasionally tipped into rough handling, and researchers recorded 13 cases in which a partner animal died, with victims including birds, pangolins, a domestic cat, and other primates. In one striking example, a male baboon in Saudi Arabia appeared to have kidnapped a domestic puppy, carrying it around for extended periods. Beyond illuminating the possible origins of human-animal companionship, researchers believe these findings carry meaningful implications for conservation and animal welfare. Understanding why certain species readily form positive relationships with others could help improve management of mixed-species environments, from wildlife sanctuaries to zoos housing multiple species in shared enclosures. The sheer range of documented behavior suggests that primates forming cross-species friendships is far more widespread than scientists had previously realized, indicating that social lives among monkeys and apes extend well beyond their own species boundaries. While these animals are not keeping pets in the deliberate, sustained way humans do today, their behaviors may represent early evolutionary building blocks eventually giving rise to the caregiving instincts and cross-species companionship that define humanity’s relationship with domesticated animals. The post Study Reveals Primates Forming Cross-Species Friendships with Dogs, Deer, and Pigs Worldwide appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A small orchard planted 13 years ago at a shuttered Kansas CIty elementary school has grown into a national movement that has inspired more than 847 orchards with 14,000 trees in 17 cities, all producing fruit for people living within walking distance. Kansas City itself now has 248 free orchards, with almost 4,600 fruit, nut and berry trees, more than any other US city. After a community gardening group in St. Louis asked for help almost a decade ago, the Giving Grove expanded into cities from Seattle to Atlanta, and is in talks with San Francisco, Minneapolis, and New York City. "It's stuff people can learn, but it takes a long time, and it's not really efficient for one group to do that," said founder Kevin Birzer. "So our thought from day one was we would provide that expertise, the knowledge of how to grow the trees, how to select the trees." The Giving Grove helps local groups find grant money, improve soil, prune trees, and work with volunteer orchard stewards. Much of its budget comes from 1% for the Planet, which mobilizes businesses to direct 1% of their annual revenue to vetted environmental solutions.

items.descriptionOriginal: Somewhere between Delhi and Kashmir, a two-and-a-half-year-old found herself waiting for tunnels to appear, pointing out sheep and monkeys by the road , and watching mountains, rivers and rain unfold outside the car window. For her parents, it was an 800-km road trip. For her, it was a moving picture book she couldn't stop asking questions about. For Akanksha Khullar, the journey had begun with a very different feeling: apprehension. Could they really drive all the way to Kashmir with a toddler? Would she manage the long hours in the car? Would the carefully planned itinerary hold up once they were on the road? Reflecting on that initial fear, Akanksha says, "It's important to show your child the possibilities that exist. And your fear is the key one." As it turned out, the daughter, whom they had worried about keeping entertained, was often the most curious traveller in the car. "She was so curious about what she was seeing and experiencing," Akanksha recalls. "There was so much greenery, so many animals just out there. She would ask, 'Which animal is this?' and then create a story around it." From tunnels and winding mountain roads to rivers and rain, the changing scenery kept Akanksha's two-and-a-half-year-old daughter curious throughout the drive. For Akanksha, a writer and storyteller who works as an advisor at the Royal Norwegian Embassy, those little questions became some of the most memorable parts of the trip. They were also what she had hoped for when the family decided to travel by road: a chance for her daughter to experience travel differently. Why they chose an 800-km drive over another flight Travel has always been a part of Akanksha and her husband's life. Their daughter had already travelled internationally, including her second international trip when she was six months old. But as Akanksha's daughter grew older and started going to day school, the family found themselves thinking differently about summer holidays. "We realised that we've only given her that international exposure," she says. "We have family throughout North India, but somehow our international trips had been more than our domestic ones." The summer holidays presented another challenge. Much of North India was hot, while popular hill stations were crowded. The couple began researching possible destinations. They considered several destinations, including Shimla and other hill stations, but Akanksha and her husband wanted to explore somewhere different this time. Rather than rushing through multiple destinations, the family kept their Kashmir itinerary limited to Srinagar and Pahalgam, allowing them to travel at a relaxed pace. "We were very sure that this time we didn't want to do a flight thing with her because we've been doing that a lot," she says. "For us, it was almost like making her relearn what travel is." That meant getting into the car and driving, maybe all the way to Kashmir. Planning the road around a toddler An 800-km road trip is a considerable journey for anyone. With a toddler, Akanksha knew they couldn't simply plan the route around distance and sightseeing. Her daughter's meals, breaks and comfort had to be part of the itinerary too. "There was a lot of strategic planning that went into the whole process," she says. They carried snacks, planned activities and thought carefully about when to start driving and where to stop. The journey was broken up according to their daughter's schedule rather than simply trying to cover as many kilometres as possible. The family was also travelling in an electric vehicle, which added another layer to the planning. Charging stops had to be factored into the journey, but some of them became enjoyable breaks for their daughter too. Charging stops during the family's electric vehicle journey became opportunities for their daughter to take a break and observe the world around her. Akanksha's husband enjoys studying cars and planning routes, so they mapped their charging stops carefully. As it turned out, several of the places where they stopped for charging also worked well for their daughter. "Having an EV and a super high-tech car is a blessing," Akanksha says. "We knew the journey was going to be very smooth." At one stop in Karnal, her daughter watched ducks. Along the route to Srinagar, the mountains, rivers and tunnels gave her plenty more to look at. Even the charging stations became memorable. On the trip, Akanksha says, her husband ended up helping other EV owners charge their cars. The biggest surprise? Their daughter loved the long drive Before leaving, one of Akanksha's biggest concerns was the car journey itself. "How is a two-and-a-half-year-old going to manage such a long journey?" was the worry. But once they were on the road, something surprising happened. "The car journey was the smoothest," she says. Her daughter was fascinated by the changing scenery. She watched the tunnels, noticed when the road went "up" and "down", looked at the rain, and kept asking questions. The journey also gave Akanksha and her husband something they don't always get on an ordinary day: uninterrupted one-on-one time with their daughter. Both parents drove, so they could split the driving. When one parent was behind the wheel, the other could sit with their daughter. Playing football on a lawn and spending uninterrupted time together became some of the simple pleasures of the trip. "She would just come up with something," Akanksha recalls. " These tiny moments that you would not get on a regular day. It was so precious." There were also moments when their daughter wanted some time with one parent. Sometimes it was "Dad, let's do this" and sometimes she would just lie down and enjoy the ride. For Akanksha, these small, unscripted moments became some of the most memorable parts of the trip. When food and motion sickness tested their plans The car journey had gone better than expected, but the trip still had its messy moments. Food, in particular, turned out to be more challenging than Akanksha had anticipated, especially in Kashmir. And on the return journey, her daughter experienced motion sickness. Thankfully, Akanksha had packed extra clothes, newspapers and bags after someone had warned her it might happen. It did. More than once. "It happened once; I changed her clothes, and then it happened again and again," she laughs, remembering the episode. By the fourth time, the parents had adapted. "We were like, okay, now we're going to sit with a flip-flop in our hand," she recalls. For Akanksha, that was another lesson in travelling with a young child: preparation matters, but so does the ability to adapt when the plan falls apart. "You learn and you adapt," she says. "It's all patience. A lot of patience. You have to centre yourself again and again." Keeping Kashmir slow Once they reached Kashmir, the family chose to keep their holiday relaxed. They kept their itinerary limited to Srinagar and Pahalgam. After all the planning and driving, Akanksha and her husband wanted a slower trip for themselves too. This gave them time to enjoy Kashmir at their own pace, with room for the little things: playing football together on a lawn, spending time as a family, and simply being present. 'You don't realise how solid a team you are as parents' Looking back, Akanksha remembers the joy alongside the challenges. She also recognises that an 800-km road trip with a toddler may not suit every family. She believes parents can sometimes underestimate what their children are capable of experiencing. "I don't know if I would advise it to anybody," she says, acknowledging that their experience was possible in part because she had a supportive partner who was completely on board. "But the point is that it's important to show your child the possibility that exists." Akanksha's family road trip to Kashmir taught them to embrace the unexpected and enjoy the journey together. For Akanksha, the biggest hurdle was her own fear. "I was very jittery. I couldn't believe that we were doing this," she says. And yet they did. The journey also gave the couple a new understanding of themselves as parents . In the busyness of everyday life, they hadn't necessarily stopped to notice how well they functioned as a team. "This whole thing gave us a lot of confidence in our journey of being parents also," she says. "You don't realise how solid a team you are as parents." Her daughter may not remember every kilometre of that 800-km journey. She may not remember the charging stations or the exact roads they took. But she saw mountains, rivers, animals and tunnels. She asked questions. She watched the world change outside the window. She spent time with both her parents. For Akanksha, those are memories she will carry with her for years. "Twenty years down the line, when I look back, I would just be like, damn. This was one good trip." All images courtesy Akanksha Khullar

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM As temperatures drop, bugs start looking for the same thing you do: somewhere warmer. If you’ve been reaching for the vinegar bottle as a first line of defense, you’re not alone. It’s an easy instinct: vinegar seems safe, familiar, and you probably already have some under the sink. Two pest management experts say the results tend to disappoint, though. Greg Baumann , founding partner of Pest Control Warrior, and Garrett Thrasher , co-owner and general manager at Thrasher Pest Control, both say vinegar works on a narrower range of pests than most people expect, and mostly not in the way people tend to use it. Where it works, and where it doesn’t Thrasher says a wet vinegar spray applied directly to a soft-bodied insect will usually kill on contact. Pantry moths, caterpillars, and mosquitoes are vulnerable to it. But vinegar evaporates quickly, and once it’s dry it does nothing to stop cockroaches, beetles, spiders, or ants. Baumann cites peer-reviewed university research showing it has negligible effects on most common household insects. “ Pests will happily walk on [wet surfaces] after vinegar evaporates,” Baumann says. “The homeowner might think it is still on the surface because the odor lingers in the air.” There’s also a surface damage problem. The acidity can strip paint finishes and stain baseboards when applied along window frames and door trim. If you want a DIY option before calling a professional, Thrasher recommends diatomaceous earth over vinegar. What the experts recommend instead Sealing works better than spraying. Caulking windows, weatherstripping doors, and adding door sweeps close off the most common entry points. Attics and crawlspaces need the same treatment. For active pest pressure around entry points, an outdoor insecticide labeled for the specific pest and location will hold up longer. Check the label to confirm it covers the right conditions for where you’re applying it. A quick walk around doors and windows once a week catches problems early, before they get in. And if you collect acorns or pine cones this fall, Thrasher recommends 30 minutes in a 150-degree Fahrenheit oven before bringing them inside. It kills any insects hiding inside them. If pests are already getting in, a professional can inspect for openings and seal them. Many pest control companies now work with low-impact products, so going professional doesn’t have to mean bringing in something harsh. Did this solution stand out? Pest experts explain what works first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
