items.description: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Η Κένυα δέσμευσε 160 εκατομμύρια δολάρια σε δέκα χρόνια για να προστατεύσει 173.000 τετραγωνικά χιλιόμετρα (περίπου 67.000 τετραγωνικά μίλια ή 17,3 εκατομμύρια εκτάρια) σε ορισμένες από τις λιγότερο διαταραγμένες εκτάσεις στην Αφρική: την κοιλάδα Great Rift, τις περιοχές Maasai Maraivers. Το πρόγραμμα ονομάζεται Thamani Asili , που σημαίνει…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Kenya committed $160 million over ten years to protect 173,000 square kilometers (roughly 67,000 square miles, or 17.3 million hectares) across some of the least-disturbed land in Africa: the Great Rift Valley, the Maasai Mara, and surrounding biodiversity areas. The program is called Thamani Asili , which means “value of nature” in Kiswahili. Funding splits evenly: $80 million from the Kenyan government, $80 million from dozens of private donors, including billionaire heirs to the Walton and Cargill family fortunes. The money flows through a Project Finance for Permanence (PFP) model, which ties disbursements to verifiable government policy changes rather than goodwill commitments. Four focus zones The initiative will start in four geographic areas. Tsavo, Kenya’s largest national park complex, holds 40 percent of the country’s elephants and 20 percent of its critically endangered black rhinos. A southern zone along the Tanzanian border spans the Maasai Mara and links into the Serengeti, a corridor that wildlife has used for seasonal migration long before either country drew its borders. The Great Rift Valley and two additional hotspots round out the four. What PFP requires Conservation funding has a recurring problem: it arrives, gets spent, and produces little that changes policy or land status. The PFP model is a structural attempt to fix that. Money is conditional on the government hitting specific policy benchmarks, not delivered up front. Brazil and Gabon signed similar agreements last year. Namibia and Botswana are in the works. Kenya’s deal is among the largest yet. Closing the 30×30 gap Kenya has committed to the global “30×30” target: 30 percent of land and sea protected by 2030. The Nature Conservancy puts current coverage at 20 to 23 percent. Ryan Bidwell, who runs TNC’s PFP program, said this deal would largely close the distance. The economic case is also there. A UN Environment Programme report drew on Kenyan government data showing that roughly 42 percent of the country’s GDP and 70 percent of its employment depend on nature in some form. Cabinet Secretary for Tourism and Wildlife Rebecca Miano said the program would benefit both wildlife and the farming communities that work these landscapes. “There is a substantial gap that would be largely closed,” Bidwell said. Whether it closes depends on Kenya delivering on the policy commitments the funding is tied to, something that’s far harder to sidestep under PFP than under a conventional grant. items.descriptionOriginal: Another exciting step forward for women’s health: Four major health societies teamed up to create the first shared framework and clinical guidance for women’s heart health, tailored to distinct life phases — from first menstruation to postmenopause. The much-needed update comes from the American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. Because while cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death in women, medical research has historically centered on men’s symptoms and physiology (which differ from women in myriad ways), thus reducing the quality of care women receive on average. This landmark move seeks to change that. The new framework organizes women’s cardiovascular care into four chronological life stages that account for hormonal and biological transitions, plus pregnancy. In addition to getting clinicians on the same page about women’s cardiovascular health, the system and its accompanying guidance can help them identify risks earlier and take necessary action before problems worsen. https://iprsoftwaremedia.com/67/files/20269/07b6ae0ca5d8a720af4942e310f02184/Dr.%20Khan%20on%20whole%20life%20view%20of%20womens%20heart%20health.mp4 “Women experience their health care across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” Dr. Sadiya S. Khan, chair of the collaborative writing group and professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, said in a news release. She noted that the updates, a trio of scientific papers published this week, “connect the dots” for providers across health domains, so holistic care can begin in adolescence. Khan added that the approach emphasizes that cardiovascular health can’t be fully understood by looking only at the heart. “We need to recognize that women’s heart health is deeply interconnected with hormonal and emotional health,” she said. The Stages Stage 1: Perimenarche The first stage comprises the transition that occurs around the first menstrual period, generally taking place between ages 8 and 15. In an essay for Time , Khan wrote that a first period before age 10 can serve as a signal of higher cardiovascular risk. “Heart health begins long before adulthood,” Dr. Amanda Marma Perak, vice-chair of the collaborative writing group and a pediatric cardiologist at Lurie Children’s Hospital, added in the news release. “As pediatric clinicians, we have the opportunity to help every girl start strong and to ensure that what we learn about her health follows her as she grows.” Stage 2: Ovarian Cycling This stage represents the approximate ages of 15-44, when regular ovulation and hormone cycles are established. Pregnancy most often occurs during these years. “Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) can frequently disrupt sleep, physical activity, and eating patterns, which are relevant to cardiovascular health,” Khan wrote for Time. “These symptoms are common, but being common does not make them inconsequential.” Heavy or irregular bleeding can also act as indicators. Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (formerly known as PCOS), for example, has been associated with a significant increase in risk for heart disease. Stage 3: Perimenopause Stage 3 represents the transition from regular to variable cycles, skipped periods, and hormone changes, taking place around ages 45-51. “Recognizing perimenopause as a distinct life stage acknowledges that its symptoms can disrupt daily life, persist for years, and deserve treatment,” wrote Khan. “Hormone and nonhormonal treatments can help, with decisions guided by symptoms, age, cardiovascular and cancer history, and a woman’s preferences. The same visit offers an opportunity to assess cardiovascular disease risk and address changes in cholesterol and cardiometabolic health.” Stage 4: Postmenopause Representing the years following menopause, which begins 12 months after one’s final period, this stage can account for 40% of a woman’s life. It occurs at approximately 51 years and older. The news release notes that most heart attacks, strokes, and heart-failure events occur during this stage — but are more than 80% preventable when steps are taken early. Pregnancy (in Any Life Stage) The framework identifies the time before, during, and after pregnancy “as a biological ‘stress test’ that can identify cardiovascular risks that may have been previously unrecognized,” per the release, which highlights postpartum care as a “missed opportunity” for many women. “Only about 60% of U.S. women with high blood pressure-related complications during pregnancy receive follow-up care for their high blood pressure within six months of delivery,” it states, noting that the American Heart Association is calling for immediate action to address that gap. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” Khan said. “Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist Reading Time: 3 minutes Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist Replacing a car is a big decision. Replacing two familiar journeys can be a smaller, more useful experiment. An e-bike may suit a trip to work, a grocery pickup, or a visit to the library without needing to handle every journey in your week. The starting question is not “How far can this bike go?” It is “Which journeys can I repeat comfortably, legally, and with a workable backup?” This checklist helps turn that question into a practical plan rather than a promise about distance, money, or carbon savings. 1. Define the two trips you want to replace Look at an ordinary week and choose journeys you currently make by car. Start with predictable destinations, manageable loads, and flexible arrival times. An appointment with no margin for delay is probably not the easiest first attempt. Be clear about counting: an outward journey and its return are two one-way trips, but one round-trip outing. Write down which definition you are using. Two bike rides do not necessarily replace two car journeys if someone still drives the same route to collect you or your shopping. 2. Find the calmer route, not just the shortest Compare a cycling map with your knowledge of local streets. Look for lower-traffic connections, suitable crossings, and routes where you feel comfortable managing the bike. A small detour may be worthwhile if it avoids a difficult junction. Inspect the awkward details: where does a bike lane end, how do you cross a busy road, and is the destination entrance accessible? Check current local rules for your bike’s class and the roads or paths you plan to use. An app’s suggested route is not proof that access is legal or conditions are suitable. 3. Budget door-to-door time Allow time to unlock the bike, load bags, negotiate crossings, park, and get ready at your destination. Do not base your schedule on the motor’s assistance cutoff or a brief top-speed reading. Neither tells you the average speed of an entire journey. Try the route without an important deadline. Record the complete travel time and how it felt, then add a buffer appropriate to your schedule. 4. Plan battery use for the whole outing Include the return leg, any errands, and a reasonable detour. Advertised maximum range is not a dependable prediction for your route. Hills, wind, temperature, assistance level, load, battery condition, and other factors can change consumption. Begin with short, familiar rides and note battery use under your own conditions. Leave a conservative reserve rather than planning to arrive empty. If charging at work is part of the plan, confirm permission and a suitable location first. Follow the bike and battery manufacturer’s charging instructions; do not assume any available charger is compatible. 5. Solve parking and carrying before leaving Know where you can lock the bike at both ends. Check whether the parking arrangement works with the frame, your lock, and the property’s rules. If stairs or lifting are involved, assess whether you can manage the bike safely before relying on that access. Pack a realistic load for a practice ride. Secure bags so they cannot interfere with steering, wheels, or braking, and respect the bike’s and rack’s stated limits. Check tire condition and pressure, brakes, lights, and load security before departure. A lighter shopping trip may be a better starting point than a weekly household shop. For a practical example focused on weekend outings, FavoriteBikes’ guide to planning e-bike errands covers stop order, bags, cargo balance, and battery margin. Adapt those planning ideas to the trips you actually want to replace. 6. Decide when not to ride Choose your fallback before you need it. Transit, rescheduling, a lift, or using the car may be appropriate when conditions exceed your ability or the bike’s limits. Check transit rules in advance, including restrictions on e-bikes, batteries, and available carrying space. Rain, darkness, strong winds, snow, and ice can change the decision. Clothing and equipment do not make every route safe, and motor assistance does not remove traction or braking risks. Avoid an unsuitable route rather than treating two weekly trips as a target that must be met regardless of conditions. 7. Keep a simple two-week record For each attempt, note the journey replaced, door-to-door time, battery use, load, conditions, and any difficulty. Include the days you chose not to ride. Those decisions help reveal whether the plan works beyond an unusually easy day. If you compare costs, distinguish avoided fuel or parking from car expenses you still pay, and include relevant bike costs. Do not assign a fixed emissions saving to every ride: the result depends on the vehicle journey actually displaced and the comparison being made. Keep the routes that fit your life, revise the difficult ones, and leave room for other transport. The useful outcome is a repeatable choice—not a perfect score or a commitment to give up the car. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News When Humans Rise, Must Another Life Fall? Rethinking Human Interests and Animal Flourishing in an Anthropocentric World Reading Time: 4 minutes If human beings rise, must other life necessarily fall? We rarely ask because we’ve never learned to see beyond ourselves, understanding that cost starts with understanding how we imagined our place in the world. Human beings have become a species capable of deciding the fate of almost everything around us: deciding where forests remain, where roads are built, where rivers flow, where wildlife may move, which animals are confined, and which habitats are altered for human purposes. Yet the power to decide does not necessarily create a right to decide. Beneath these choices lies an anthropocentric hierarchy where human interests are treated as primary while the interests of other living beings are considered secondary whenever they conflict with human preferences. Against this hierarchy, I rely on Martha C. Nussbaum’s capabilities approach to examine whether human interests should automatically prevail when their pursuit restricts the fundamental capabilities of animals. In Justice for Animals: Our Collective Responsibility , Martha places animals in the sphere of justice and argues that justice requires more than preventing suffering. It requires securing the conditions necessary for animals to flourish according to their species-specific nature. The precise content of flourishing necessarily differs between each species. A bird requires opportunity to fly, a fish requires an aquatic environment in which it can swim and behave according to its nature, and a wild animal requires habitat, movement, ecological relationships, and the ability to exist without constant human control. For Martha, the problem is not simply suffering. It is capability deprivation. The human domination over animals is not accidental; it is structural and deeply embodied in our political, cultural, social, and economic systems. It does not arise merely from individual cruelty but from institutional arrangements designed around human benefits. Around the world, animal laws and conservation policies are structured within an anthropocentric framework. Animals are protected, conserved, and regulated not as right-bearing beings, but as resources to be managed for human benefits. Like, in Pakistan, animals are largely protected through welfare-based laws, not through a capabilities-based framework. The primary legislation, such as the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1890 largely focuses on preventing visible cruelty rather than ensuring the flourishing of animals. Similarly, the provincial laws prioritize conservation of wildlife for human benefit rather than justice for animals themselves. The absence of a capabilities-based legal framework means that animals are still treated as objects of ownership and trade. Fish and birds sold on Pakistani streets are not perceived as beings whose rights are violated; instead, they are seen as commodities. They are viewed as property rather than beings of justice, where exploitation becomes habitual, invisible, and unquestioned. Human interests are not morally uniform. Human beings require food, shelter, health, security, transportation, livelihood, and infrastructure. But human societies also pursue convenience, entertainment, aesthetic preferences, commercial profits, and cultural habits. These interests cannot carry the same moral weight. A preference for cheap entertainment cannot automatically be placed on the same level as an animal’s basic freedom of movement. Fish trapped inside transparent plastic bags, under the complete control of a fish vendor on the streets of Lahore. Their aquatic life is reduced to a small plastic world where they remain alive, but are deprived of the space and freedom to live according to their nature. Photo by the author. Commercial tourism cannot automatically justify disturbing wildlife. Infrastructure development cannot justify destroying habitat where an alternative route or design is available. Martha’s framework, combined with necessity and proportionality principle, distinguishes the moral weight of different human claims. First, the human interest must be legitimate and sufficiently important. Secondly, the particular interference with animal capabilities must actually be necessary to achieve that interest. Lastly, where a less harmful and reasonable alternative exists, the more harmful practice should not be permitted merely because it is cheaper, easier, or customary. These tests distinguish human interests into non-essential, significant but non-vital, and vital human interests. Martha makes it clear that unnecessary human interests carry no moral or legal exception when they exploit an animal’s capabilities. Zoo confinement is a clear example of how entertainment and profit function as human interests that undermine animal rights. These animals are removed from their natural habitats and placed in artificial, restrictive environments, often in noisy and polluted urban settings. Zoos deny their freedom of movement, bodily integrity, and natural behavior’s, reducing them to spectacles for human amusement and revenue generation. The same analysis applies to the roadside sale of birds and fish. Birds confined in cages and fish sold in plastic bags are alive but incapable of flourishing. Even when sellers claim livelihood necessity, this interest remains non-essential because alternative businesses are available. The human right to business or livelihood cannot justify the exploitation of sentient beings. When business models depend on violating animal capabilities, they are illegal and should be prohibited. Justice requires banning such practices and supporting alternative livelihoods that do not rely on animal suffering. The commercial activities in protected wildlife areas reflect another form of human interest. Glamping and overcrowding disrupt wildlife migration patterns, feeding habits, breeding cycles, and freedom. While it generates profits, these benefits are not necessary for human survival and cannot justify the erosion of animal capabilities. Deforestation and unchecked urbanization also conflict with animals flourishing. They are built upon a hierarchy that privileges human expansion over interspecies justice. When forests and green belts are cleared for commercial use, animals lose the ecological foundation necessary for their existence. Habitat destruction fragments ecosystems, eliminates nesting and breeding grounds, and increases starvation and human-wildlife conflict. When forests are valued only for timber, and land and rivers are valued for commercial use, animals are reduced to externalities. In these cases, the principle is clear: human interest must be necessary and regulated. Economic gain, entertainment, and convenience cannot justify the deprivation of animal capabilities, particularly when alternatives exist or when such practices serve no essential human needs. If animal exploitation becomes normal and the state fails to regulate unnecessary human interests, the animal’s existence will become impossible. The limitation on human interests does not mean eliminating human freedom, but it means regulating and restricting activities that commodify living beings unnecessarily. Martha’s theory reminds us that animals are not objects of convenience; they are subjects whose capabilities impose limits on our ambition. The fish trapped in plastic, birds in cages, and zoo animals remind us that flourishing is a right, not a privilege, and human interest, no matter how convenient or profitable, must stop where the capabilities of other sentient beings begin. Limiting unnecessary and exploitative human interests is not a moral preference but a legal obligation in a just society committed to interspecies dignity and coexistence. It underscores that human freedom, while important, is not absolute and must yield when it conflicts with the flourishing of other species. The post When Humans Rise, Must Another Life Fall? Rethinking Human Interests and Animal Flourishing in an Anthropocentric World appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Sustainable Polymers and Natural Rubber Chart a Path Toward Greener Materials Reading Time: 3 minutes Sustainable polymers and natural rubber are moving to the center of materials science, as new research shows how to design them to reduce their environmental footprint. Sustainable polymers and natural rubber took center stage at a joint symposium between researchers in France and Thailand. The University of Haute-Alsace and Kasetsart University co-hosted the online event across May 2026. The program covered a wide range of materials topics, from energy materials to nanotechnology. One theme stood out clearly across the sessions. Scientists are now designing polymers not just for performance, but for durability, repairability, and better end-of-life outcomes. Dr. Wirasak Smitthipong of Kasetsart University presented one of the symposium’s central ideas. His team studies smart polymers that respond to light and can heal themselves when damaged. These self-healing materials include rubber and hydrogel systems. Special molecular bonds allow damaged sections to reconnect and recover their function, much like scar tissue mending itself. That self-repair ability matters beyond the lab. If a material can signal damage and fix itself, it may not need replacing as often. This applies especially to coatings, adhesives, and composite products, where small damage often forces the replacement of a much larger item. Light also played a starring role in another presentation. Dr. Jacques Lalevée from the Institut de Science des Matériaux de Mulhouse, part of the University of Haute-Alsace, discussed new light-activated processing methods for high-performance materials. His work uses light to trigger chemical reactions in coatings, inks, adhesives, and 3D-printed parts. This approach offers precise control, produces little or no volatile organic compound release, and reacts faster than older methods. That same light-based technique can work with bio-based resins made from natural oils. This points toward manufacturing that uses less energy and allows for localized repairs rather than full replacement. Other researchers tackled the opposite end of a material’s life. Dr. Amornrat Lertworasirikul of Kasetsart University studies how to make polylactic acid, a common bio-based plastic known as PLA, break down more easily after use. PLA already appears in packaging, farming tools, and medical devices. Her team found that adding a small amount, just 3% by weight, of a plant-derived compound helped the plastic become more flexible and degrade faster in water. This research raises an important question for sustainable polymers and natural rubber alike. Should a material last for decades, break down quickly, or simply become easier to repair and reuse? The answer depends entirely on the product. Packaging that gets used once benefits from fast degradation, while structural materials benefit more from durability and repair options. Natural rubber also showed plenty of untapped potential. Sustainable polymers and natural rubber face the same fundamental design question: should a material last for decades, break down quickly, or be easier to repair and reuse? The new research shows that a 3% plant-derived additive can make plastic more flexible and water-degradable, suggesting the answer depends entirely on what the material is made to do. Photo by Lucas van Oort on Unsplash. Dr. Sutee Boonchui presented transparent, flexible films made by blending natural rubber with quantum dots, tiny particles that glow under light. These fluorescent films could improve road safety equipment, making traffic signs and markers more visible. The natural rubber base keeps the material flexible enough for real-world outdoor use. Medical safety also got a rubber-based upgrade. Dr. Kiadtisak Saenboonruang described multilayer gloves made from sustainable polymers and natural rubber, designed to block X-ray radiation more effectively. By layering in a nanoscale bismuth oxide additive, the gloves blocked more radiation than standard single-layer versions. The outer layers of pure natural rubber kept the gloves flexible and comfortable to wear. Tire manufacturing also came under the sustainability lens. Dr. Hassarutai Yangthong showed how fly ash, a waste byproduct from burning coal, can replace some of the zinc oxide typically used in tire rubber production. Zinc oxide use raises environmental concerns when it washes into waterways. Lifecycle analysis found that substituting fly ash lowered several measures of environmental harm, including toxicity to freshwater and marine life. Taken together, these projects reveal a shared philosophy. True sustainability depends on a material’s entire lifecycle, not simply whether it originates from renewable sources. A bio-based plastic that requires enormous energy to produce offers little advantage over conventional options. Likewise, a material that degrades too quickly may not suit long-term applications like construction or safety equipment. Sustainable polymers and natural rubber research is now moving toward this more complete picture. Scientists are learning to weigh performance, repairability, and lifespan together rather than treating them as separate goals. The symposium’s researchers plan to keep exploring how far these smart materials can go. As industries search for greener alternatives to conventional plastics and rubber, this kind of integrated thinking may prove essential to getting the balance right. The post Sustainable Polymers and Natural Rubber Chart a Path Toward Greener Materials appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Bat Conservation Books Offer Something for Every Age Reading Time: 3 minutes From picture books for toddlers to a 400-page field guide, new bat conservation books invite readers of every age into the surprisingly wondrous world of the only flying mammal. Bat conservation books rarely dominate bestseller lists, but a fresh crop of titles released this year proves the subject deserves far more shelf space than it typically gets. Bat Conservation International recently rounded up a dozen standout titles spanning children’s picture books to dense scientific references, each aiming to replace fear of bats with fascination. For younger readers, several bat conservation books lean into storytelling and gentle life lessons. Stellaluna, considered among the first children’s books centered on bats, follows a baby fruit bat raised temporarily among birds after falling from her mother’s roost, ultimately learning that differences need not prevent friendship. I’m Not Scary follows a lonely bat who simply wants companionship despite living somewhere admittedly spooky, offering warm illustrations built around a familiar theme: kindness overcoming fear. Other bat conservation books for children tackle real conservation challenges directly. Bat Count: A Citizen Science Story introduces young readers to white-nose syndrome, the disease that has devastated North American bat populations, following a girl preparing for a community bat count who learns both the crisis facing bats and how ordinary people can help through citizen science. Amara and the Bats follows a similar arc, as a young bat enthusiast discovers her new neighborhood’s bat roosts have vanished due to tree removal, then finds inspiration in other young people already working to protect local bat populations. Additional titles for younger audiences round out the reading list. Little Red Bat explores the dilemma facing bat species that must choose between migration and hibernation as autumn arrives, weaving in facts about tree-roosting habits and camouflage along the way. The Bat Book, narrated from the perspective of a juvenile bat living under a bridge in Austin, Texas, directly addresses common misconceptions children repeat about bats being weird or scary. For adult readers and dedicated naturalists, bat conservation books shift toward deeper scientific territory. The Secret Lives of Bats follows renowned bat photographer and biologist Merlin Tuttle’s decades-long career, beginning with a teenage cave discovery outside Knoxville, Tennessee, that launched a lifetime devoted to bat ecology and conservation across encounters ranging from Kentucky moonshiners to charging elephants. The Weird and Wonderful World of Bats takes a curiosity-driven approach, devoting individual chapters to each bat sense, including echolocation, alongside candid explorations of bat mating behavior and social communication. For naturalists and dedicated readers, recent bat conservation books like Bats of the World: A Guide to Every Family and Bat Island document the diversity of nearly 1,500 known bat species through detailed photography, distribution maps, and firsthand field research. Photo courtesy of Bat Conservation International . The Genius Bat follows an ecologist’s research travels from Israeli deserts to tropical rainforests, examining how scientists design experiments to study bats’ extraordinary sensory and behavioral adaptations. For readers wanting comprehensive identification resources, bat conservation books like Bats of the World: A Guide to Every Family organize the roughly 1,500 known bat species by suborder, pairing close-up photography with distribution maps and details on diet, anatomy, and physiology. Bat Island narrows its focus dramatically, documenting the 76 bat species found on a single small island in Panama’s Lake Gatun through cinematic photography and firsthand research from Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute scientists. Rounding out the collection, Bats: An Illustrated Guide to All Species offers a 400-page reference dividing global bat diversity along modern phylogenetic lines, paired with extensive photography documenting species across every studied region. Together, these bat conservation books reflect a broader shift in how bats are represented in popular literature, moving decisively away from Halloween-season stereotypes toward genuine appreciation for animals that pollinate plants, disperse seeds, and consume enormous quantities of agricultural pests nightly. Whether introducing a child to their first bat-loving picture book character or offering seasoned naturalists a comprehensive species reference, this year’s releases make clear that meaningful conservation storytelling can also be genuinely engaging reading, proving that getting curious about bats might be the easiest first step toward protecting them. The post Bat Conservation Books Offer Something for Every Age appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Το πείραμα του Business School χωρίς τιμές
items.titleOriginal: The Business School Experiment with No Prices
items.description: Νωρίς στο σχολείο, ο Gaurav Marathe αγκάλιασε ένα μάντρα Viraja που μεταφράστηκε από έναν δάσκαλο: "Οι άνθρωποι είναι σαν ένα κερί. Αφού καεί το κερί, ο άνθρακας μένει πάνω του, και πρέπει να αφαιρέσετε αυτόν τον μαύρο άνθρακα από το φως, ώστε το φως να ανάψει ξανά." Το μάντρα του έμαθε να πειραματίζεται τόσο με την αφαίρεση του άνθρακα όσο και με το φωτισμό του jyoti -- το φως…
items.descriptionOriginal: Early on in school, Gaurav Marathe embraced a Viraja mantra translated by a teacher: "Humans are like a candle. After the candle burns, carbon stays on it, and you have to remove that black carbon from the light so the light again illuminates." The mantra taught him to experiment with both removing the carbon and illuminating the jyoti -- the light that exists within. In one of many experiments, he challenged students to remove the carbon of a task-driven, rule-driven festival on a campus where he taught. "Let's do that experiment. Let it be the kind of carnival where nobody is charging anything. No cost price, nothing. If anybody wants to pay, they pay. If they don't, they don't. Let's believe in that spirit." It was successful beyond anyone's imagination, and became a "Soul Carnival" where the focus is on giving over profiting. "Perhaps that's the point of these experiments — not to have all the answers, but to keep creating spaces where we can go close to inner jyoti a little more."

items.titleOriginal: Student Makers, a deeper dive: bringing free STEM to students on three continents
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Αυτό το άρθρο ξεκινά τη σειρά Local Changemakers 2026 του The Optimist Daily, δίνοντας έμφαση στους δημιουργούς αλλαγής 30 ετών και κάτω. Ο πατέρας του ετοίμαζε τις βαλίτσες του για ένα ταξίδι αποστολής στην Κένυα, όπου ήταν εθελοντής με την Kenya Relief , έναν ιατρικό οργανισμό που διευθύνει ένα scho…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article kicks off The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. It was winter break, and Dilan Mehta had time on his hands. His dad was packing for a mission trip to Kenya, where he’d been volunteering with Kenya Relief , a medical organization that runs a school in Migori, for years. Dilan packed a bag of stuffed animals for the children there. Then he glanced at his 3D printer. He started designing LEGO-inspired sets, printing each one out, and tucking them in alongside the stuffed animals. Somewhere between one print and the next, a different thought took shape. The school had students who could use a curriculum, and his dad had room in a suitcase. That’s how a 3D printer ended up in Migori, Kenya, and why it’s still being used to teach students today. What is Student Makers? Student Makers is a nonprofit that offers free STEM workshops to students across the United States, Kenya, and India, and every instructor is a former student. Most of them are still in high school. The organization was founded in California in 2019 by Anthony Neil Tan, then a high school senior. There was no space at his school where students interested in technology and making could come together to learn, so he built one. He called it the Maker Hub Club Initiative, secured a $5,000 grant from a social impact scholarship, and got it off the ground. The framework was three steps: learn a skill , make a project, showcase it. He was in his first year of college when he started handing it off. Serve: the fourth pillar Dilan didn’t find Student Makers; rather, Anthony found him. Roughly six years ago, Dilan was only in 8th grade and had entered an Autodesk design contest with a 3D-printed fingerboard, one that used flexible filament on the grip surface to behave like rubber. Anthony came across it and reached out. Would Dilan want to join a group where students build things and learn from each other? He joined, took the 3D printing course, came back as an instructor, and eventually rebuilt the entire curriculum from scratch around design thinking rather than output. A few years later, he was running the organization. But he felt that the project’s mission needed some rethinking. The original framework had three steps: learn, make, showcase. Dilan added a fourth, serve, because the workshops were primarily reaching students who already had resources, and that wasn’t what he’d signed up for. His dad’s Kenya-bound suitcase gave him the opening for a bigger idea to launch. Teaching through rain and static When Dilan sent that 3D printer to Kenya Relief Academy, he wasn’t thinking about it as a program. He was thinking about a school with 800 students, roughly 170 to 190 of them orphaned children, consistently ranked the top primary school in its region out of more than 800, and without any STEM infrastructure. His dad’s Kenya Relief contacts connected him to the teachers there, and he started meeting with them remotely three times a week. Every session ran over video call, Dilan in the US and the teachers in Migori, and when the Wi-Fi dropped, which it often would, they’d wait, reconnect, and keep going. He trained them in Autodesk Fusion 360, Tinkercad, and 3D printer operation, working through how to teach all of it to a classroom he’s never seen in person. “They constantly have Wi-Fi issues,” Dilan said. “Anytime there’s rain, they basically lose connection. Just being patient, being empathetic , understanding that that’s just the situation.” Ruth Agongo, a teacher at Kenya Relief Academy, described what it looked like from the other end. “You are a game-changer,” she said. “Whatever you have taught us, we are putting into action because the kids are really excited by the technology.” Jacob A few semesters into his time at Georgia Tech, once Dilan had actually taken a step back from Student Makers and was serving mostly as an advisory board member, Dilan got a message from the teachers at Kenya Relief Academy. They needed help with a science fair project: an Arduino-based robot that could navigate a garden, measure soil moisture at different points, and decide where to water. Dilan didn’t know much about robotics, but he was at Georgia Tech, so he asked around. Twelve students from the university ended up on the project. They built components in Atlanta while the Kenya team built in Migori, troubleshot over video call, and sent physical supplies through a similar suitcase network that had carried the original printer. That team placed third at regionals of the Kenya Science and Engineering Fair. One of the students on it, a ninth-grader named Jacob, now leads Kenya Relief Academy’s robotics team. His dream is to become a rocket engineer at NASA. A family connection in India Rohan Naegle, who led Student Makers before the current team took over, brought a similar program to Dr. R.V. Shah English Medium School in rural Gujarat, India, after his grandfather put him in touch with the school. Live 3D printing classes run there over video call, using the same structure. More than 25 secondary students have completed the program, and a donated printer stays at the school. Both the Kenya and India connections came organically, through family. How the pipeline runs Aarush Goel, who now leads the high school chapters, came in the same way Dilan did: a friend pulled him in to co-teach a Python workshop, and he showed up not entirely sure what he was doing. “You just start teaching and everything goes into place,” he said. He’s since led five workshop tracks across the US, and next year he’ll start a Student Makers chapter at his own college. Instructors are recruited the same way at every level. At the end of each cycle, a call goes out for anyone who wants to come back and teach the next round. Usually one or two students say yes. They already know the program from the inside, which tends to make them good at the part that matters most: building something new students actually want to stay in. Anthony, watching from his current advisory role, put it plainly. “It’s more relatable, a high schooler showing a middle schooler how to do some 3D printing than someone who’s already a young adult,” he said. “So it’s nice keeping that peer-to-peer instruction model.” He’s 25. The organization he started as a high school senior just turned seven. Growing the network Student Makers recently joined a partnership with Youth Technology Corps Global Alliance , a network of schools across roughly 12 countries that has been running a similar peer-learning model since 1998. YTC has been doing this for nearly three decades and has school connections worldwide; Student Makers brings the volunteers and the curriculum. This fall, programs are launching under the partnership in Mexico, Colombia, Ethiopia, and Illinois, with the 3D printing and CAD curriculum going into Mexico specifically. “I would have never imagined that we would have this extensive of a reach,” Anthony said. The reach he couldn’t have imagined started with a simple observation: students interested in technology and making didn’t have a space to come together. So he built one. Why Student Makers opens this year’s series Each year, The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers series runs in the weeks before Thanksgiving, and this year, for the first time, every person in it is 30 or under. When Aarush reached out to us with the Student Makers story last summer, we spent weeks talking with the people who built this organization and were honestly floored by their dedication, hard work, and willingness to serve others. The five other changemakers in this year’s series were nominated by The Optimist Daily community, but Student Makers was not. It was the story that inspired the decision behind this year’s “30 and under” theme. This article skims the surface of the deeper story behind Student Makers. If you want to learn more about their incredible work, hang tight for a podcast episode featuring the voices behind this initiative. It’ll be coming out in early 2027. In the meantime, you can learn more and support their work at www.studentmakers.org . The post Student Makers, a deeper dive: bringing free STEM to students on three continents first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. Most social programs ask you to declare yourself before they’ll give you anything. You fill out a form, check a box, explain your circumstances to someone with authority over the outcome. Vivian Ho built All The Same Organization around the idea that this moment, identifying yourself as someone who needs help, was what kept people from asking at all. Vivian lives in Cedar Park, Texas, but the organization operates nationally. She is, remarkably, only 17 years old. ATS delivers supply packages directly to low-income families through Title I schools: food, hygiene products, household necessities, school supplies. Families request what they need through an anonymous sign-up system. No one who receives support is required to name themselves as the recipient. “Just because resources exist does not mean that it’s accessible,” wrote Anika Luangaphay, who co-founded ATS alongside Vivian. The anonymous system, Luangaphay explained, was designed to let families “choose what type of support they want” without attaching their identity to the request. Volunteers with the All The Same Organization Reaching Title I families across the country Since its founding, ATS has grown to more than 200 chapters with roughly 8,000 volunteers and has distributed over 150,000 supplies to families at Title I schools. In a single back-to-school season , the organization served five schools and delivered more than 15,000 school supplies. Vendor events in the Austin and Cedar Park area have raised more than $75,000 in goods. ATS brings supplies directly to schools, removing the need for families to travel. Outreach is conducted across language barriers so that immigrant families can find and navigate the program without information being another wall to get over. Aoto Yamazaki, a longtime volunteer, described Vivian’s approach as incredibly empathetic and well-thought-out: “What makes Vivian’s work especially meaningful to me is how intentionally she considers each student’s culture due to her past experiences as an immigrant.” Cultural Surprises Cultural Surprises works like this: volunteers research the cultural background of a recipient family, then create handmade arts and crafts based on what they find. The crafts go out alongside the supply packages. More than 500 crafts have been made for over 60 recipients. Volunteers don’t just pack boxes; they do the work to understand the people they’re packing for. Yamazaki wrote that the program had changed what he understood about volunteering: “Being part of this work has taught me so much about cultures I previously knew little about, including Hmong culture.” Luangaphay connected it directly to Vivian’s own history. “She had told me herself that she grew up suppressing her culture due to being a Vietnamese immigrant,” Luangaphay wrote, “so now she recognizes the students in Title I schools often neglect their own culture, too.” The crafts are partly a way of giving back something that growing up between cultures tends to cost. ATS has now secured funding for a Cultural Spotlight Scholarship. Rather than asking volunteers to make crafts for recipients, this program invites students to create art and crafts inspired by their own cultures, with a short written description of what the piece means and where it comes from. Those descriptions get shared with a wider audience. Winners will receive $1,250. The goal, as Luangaphay described it, is to give participants “a deep dive into a culture, whether it’s their own or another person’s.” A classroom, and what came after After noticing a gap in career exposure at the schools she worked with, Vivian fundraised for medical supplies, including mannequins, suture kits, and stethoscopes, then developed a partnership with Age of Central Texas to build a functional medical classroom at Dobie Middle School. When the school went through a turnaround and that classroom was shut down, she turned her attention to other Title I schools rather than walking away. “Her willingness to keep finding ways to help, even when her original efforts did not go as planned, is something that has always stayed with me,” Yamazaki wrote. Yamazaki saw the same thing in smaller moments. Early in his time with the organization, he told Vivian he wanted to start his own project after being inspired by her work. “She selflessly gave me her time, advice, and guidance, walking me through how to turn my ideas into something that could create a real impact,” he wrote. She was, at that point, a teenager running a multi-chapter national nonprofit. Vivian received two nominations for this series: one from her co-founder and one from a volunteer she inspired to build something of his own. Both of them described an organization built on one idea: that people should be able to ask for help without giving anything of themselves away to get it. Learn more and get involved at www.allthesame.org . Vivian Ho, founder. Πολλές από αυτές τις πόλεις r…
items.descriptionOriginal: From the deep South to colonial New England, certain U.S. locales have developed chilling reputations for reports of apparitions and other paranormal activity. Long shadows have been cast by histories steeped in calamity, and stories abound of restless souls condemned to cemeteries and peevish poltergeists with bones to pick. Many of these cities relish their notoriety, with multiple laying claim to the title of most haunted in the country. We detail a few of them below, but whether you use this list as a roster of places you dare not enter or as a resource for your next vacation, proceed with caution: We can’t promise that reading our roundup won’t summon the spirits mentioned within it. Savannah, Georgia Glen Richard—iStock/Getty Images Plus Savannah offers all the charm of the South and all the unease of a Southern Gothic novel — if you know where to look. Lurking amid the oak-lined streets and majestic mansions are specters borne of centuries of tragedy (or so the story goes). Founded in 1733, the city played major roles in the Revolutionary and Civil Wars and was ravaged by several yellow fever outbreaks in the 1800s. The souls lost in those events are said to haunt Savannah’s historic cemeteries and buildings. “Visitors and locals alike report unexplained phenomena across Savannah: sudden cold spots, shadow figures, voices, apparitions, and objects moving without cause,” claims local hotel Bellwether House, which was built in 1876. “Ghost sightings aren’t confined to one building — they’re woven into the city itself.” Even its own chamber of commerce boasts its reputation as “the most haunted city in America” (a title New Orleans also claims). Check out 10 of the spookiest places in Savannah. Atchison, Kansas DonsESLAdventure—iStock Editorial/Getty Images Plus Known for being the birthplace of Amelia Earhart , Atchison’s other claim to fame is its purported paranormal activity. Situated on the Missouri River, it’s home to the infamous Sallie House . Legend has it that after a young girl named Sallie died there during a failed appendicitis operation in 1905, her ghost stuck around. Though locals had long considered the abode haunted, the story truly took hold in 1993 when a couple moved in and began experiencing ominous phenomena — including a fire, objects moving around on their own, and unexplained scratches. Other eerie sites in Atchison (called “America’s most haunted town” by its tourism department) include the McInteer Villa , an 1889 Victorian mansion that’s elicited reports of supernatural occurrences; the Rose Trunk Building , where visitors have claimed they sensed an unseen presence; and Benedictine College, said to be haunted by the spirits of monks who founded it over 150 years ago. New Orleans, Louisiana lightphoto—iStock/Getty Images Plus Welcome to New Orleans, a 308-year-old city rife with historical trauma. Its early days were marked by violence and sorrow, which continued into the 19th century as slavery, the Civil War, and several disease outbreaks took their toll. A merging of West African spiritual practices and Catholicism gave rise to its distinct voodoo tradition , and today, “the line between the living and the dead often feels surprisingly thin,” per the city’s tourism department. If you’re looking for a hair-raising time, you should certainly visit the French Quarter. Book a stay at the Andrew Jackson Hotel — believed to be haunted by five boys who perished there in a fire when it was a boarding school — or dine at Antoine’s Restaurant, reportedly home to 19th-century spirits who peer out from the bathroom mirrors. The ghost of author William Faulkner is said to remain in the rooms he rented in the neighborhood, which have since been converted into a bookstore called Faulkner House Books. Learn about more haunted places in New Orleans. Salem, Massachusetts AndTheyTravel—iStock Editorial / Getty Images Plus Salem’s dark history has seemingly cast a spell over the colonial New England town. The area’s notorious witch trials saw around 200 people accused of witchcraft in the 1690s. About 30 were found guilty and at least 19 were put to death. Today, this chilling past resurfaces in reports of ghost sightings and other supernatural phenomena. Proctor’s Ledge , the trials’ primary execution site, is said to be haunted, with visitors reporting cold spots, incandescent orbs, and a disembodied voice, per Ghost City Tours. The Joshua Ward House , built on the site where George Corwin — High Sheriff during the witch trials — once lived, is also the stuff of legend: An accused man named Giles Corey is rumored to have cursed Corwin and the town of Salem with his final breath during his execution. At the Old Burying Point Cemetery , established in 1637, condemned souls are believed to be responsible for mysterious shadows, noises, mist, and an overwhelming sense of despair. Anoka, Minnesota Officially known as “the Halloween Capital of the World,” Anoka is rich with tales of the paranormal. Reportedly haunted buildings include the Anoka State Hospital , a psychiatric institution that opened in 1900; Colonial Hall, where furniture is said to move around inexplicably after dark; and the old Anoka library, with a known history of “books flying off of shelves,” per local outlet HometownSource. The Anoka County Historical Society, which formerly used the library as its headquarters, offers guided ghost tours that are “60% history, 40% folklore” and based on real stories from the people who live and work in the city’s buildings. Virginia City, Nevada NNehring—E+/Getty Images “To say everything is haunted in this old mining town is not too far from the truth,” proclaims Virginia City’s tourism department. The locale topped the ranking in the 2026 Spookiest Cities Report , a playful analysis by home security company Vivint. The ranking used seven measures, adjusted for population: haunted places, ghost sightings, funeral services, haunted houses, psychics and astrologers, spiritual shops, and spooky Google search volume. Visitors can explore eerie places like the Gold Hill Hotel, Nevada’s oldest, where rumors persist of children’s ghosts running the halls, or bring home a bottle of Cemetery Gin, the city’s own distilled spirit. This month — dubbed Hauntober — one of the area’s top ghost experts is leading paranormal investigations at the historic St. Mary’s Art Center, which was originally a hospital and is known as one of Virginia City’s most haunted buildings. Gettysburg, Pennsylvania pabradyphoto— iStock/Getty Images Plus The Civil War’s Battle of Gettysburg in 1863 resulted in over 50,000 casualties, and many believe that the spirits of the soldiers who died on the battlefield remain there, reliving the brutal conflict. For over 100 years, visitors and locals have reported “phantom footsteps, ghostly drumbeats, and echoes of musket fire and cannon blasts,” per History . Other spots in the city, widely known as one of the country’s most haunted places , have their own eerie history tied to the war. The Jennie Wade House Museum commemorates, and is said to be possessed by, the only civilian killed in the battle. Visitors have claimed to hear whispers, feel cold spots, and see Wade’s ghost floating through the rooms. Those daring enough to walk into the Sachs Covered Bridge — where a trio of Confederate soldiers were executed for impersonating Union troops — may encounter three disembodied heads or feel phantom fingers tapping their shoulders.

Και μοιράζονται μερικές υπέροχες εικόνες και βίντεο στη διαδικασία. Μια νέα μελέτη από το Κέντρο Χάρβαρντ και Σμιθσόνιαν…
items.descriptionOriginal: What happened after the Big Bang? A team of physicists, harnessing the James Webb and Nancy Grace Roman space telescopes, are working to visualize the answer to that question using a novel computer simulation called Lumina. And they’re sharing some pretty stellar images and videos in the process. A new study out of the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics introduces Lumina, which provides an unprecedented look at how the universe may have formed. The simulation harkens back to the nascent universe, from the dark ages that followed the Big Bang through the next 2 billion years of cosmic evolution. “The early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” lead author Oliver Zier said in a statement , crediting the James Webb scope. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video.” Lumina collaboration A visualization of hydrogen re-ionization Those predictions focus on how the first galaxies, stars, and other cosmic structures were able to form amid a period of total darkness. Per a press release from MIT, the effect of the Big Bang was such that no light or radiation could pass through the “shroud” of neutral hydrogen created by the rapid expansion event. Eventually, however, two massive transformations occurred: the re-ionization of hydrogen and the re-ionization of helium. Hydrogen re-ionization refers to the era when the first stars were able to emit enough ultraviolet light to strip the neutral hydrogen of its electrons, preventing it from absorbing photons and thus “allowing light to travel freely.” Similarly, helium re-ionization refers to the breaking apart of neutral helium via high-energy light, something thought to have been fueled by supermassive black holes. The simulation captures these two essential processes in detail for the first time. Lumina collaboration A visualization of helium re-ionization “Lumina does everything from small-scale star and galaxy formation to large-scale re-ionization of hydrogen and helium, in a volume that is 100 times larger than previous best simulations,” study co-author Mark Vogelsberger said in the press release. He added the detail is unparalleled: “Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this. The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation.” Looking ahead, the team is making Lumina available to the scientific community to compare its simulations with real-world snapshots taken by new and future telescopes and tell a more complete story of how the first galaxies, stars, and structures of the universe may have formed. items.descriptionOriginal: People are drowning in eco-friendly swag—cloth tote bags, reusable water bottles, recycled notebooks, sustainable hotel toiletries, and on and on—distributed by organizations and companies eager to demonstrate their environmental bona fides. What might be even more sustainable than manufacturing and distributing all these eco-friendly products is to just…stop. The trouble is that consumers have trouble giving brands credit for such restraint, a quirk of human psychology that researchers dub “sustainable additive bias” in a new paper. “Companies that genuinely try to take eco-friendly actions, such as reducing packaging or promotional giveaways, are often not rewarded,” says study team member Linda Lemarié , associate professor of marketing at Audencia Business School in France. “What we don’t see is hard to take into consideration, and reduction leaves nothing visible, even though it’s often the best strategy from an environmental standpoint.” In the paper, Lemarié and her colleagues conducted nine different studies to demonstrate how this bias works—and what companies can do about it. The studies included a field experiment in which hotel guests rated the sustainability of the room they had stayed in, a lab experiment in which business school students chose gifts to hand out to trade show attendees, and seven online investigations in which a total of more than 2,900 participants were asked to evaluate complimentary hotel toiletries, hair care sets, music festival welcome bags, and other collections of products. Overall, the studies show that consumers see businesses as more sustainable when they provide more eco-friendly items rather than when they remove unnecessary ones—even though subtracting can lead to true: Information that confirms your beliefs...or information repeated over and over? “We were first surprised by the robustness and consistency of the effect across different contexts and with different metrics,” Lemarié says. For example, study participants judged a hotel room stocked with a large selection of eco-friendly toiletries as more sustainable than a room with a more modest set of eco-friendly products. They also judged a limited-edition tea box to which eco-friendly tea filters had been added as more sustainable than one from which they had been removed. “Then we were also surprised by the bias’s resistance to knowledge,” Lemarié says. When items weren’t labeled as being environmentally friendly , participants identified bundles with more items as being less sustainable than those with fewer. “This means that people do indeed correctly associate ‘addition with ‘less environmentally friendly.’” But when the question of sustainability comes into play, people seem to use visible components as indicators of companies’ effort. The more items, the more effort, and the more effort, the more sustainability—at least, according to our imperfect brains. Several of the experiments suggest sustainable additive bias can be counteracted when companies prioritize highly recognizable items as sustainability signals (that is, a refillable water bottle counts more than biodegradable glitter). One hints that explaining when items have been removed for environmental reasons might help, too. But accomplishing this in the real world could be tricky, Lemarié says. “The question our research leaves open is how to effectively demonstrate, without appearing hypocritical or making people skeptical, that reducing elements of a product offering, and thus offering less, is a genuine effort in favor of the environment.” Source: Lemarié L. et al. “ The more, the better?
